Given at 298 K :

$\begin{aligned} & E_{Fe^{2+}/Fe}^{\circ}=X\text{Volt} \\ & E_{Fe^{3+}/Fe}^{\circ}=Y\text{Volt} \end{aligned}$

The $E_{Fe^{3+}/Fe^{2+}}^{\circ}$ in Volt at 298 K is given by :
questions.explanation_text: (i) $Fe^{+2}(aq)+2e^{-} \rightarrow Fe(s)\dots\dots..\Delta G_{1}^{\circ}$ (ii) $Fe^{+3}(aq)+3e^{-} \rightarrow Fe(s)\dots\dots..\Delta G_{2}^{\circ}$ (iii) $Fe^{+3}(aq)+e^{-} \rightarrow Fe^{+2}(aq)\dots\dots..\Delta G_{3}^{\circ}$ $\begin{aligned} & \text{iii}=\text{ii}-i \\ & -1 \times F \times E_{Fe^{3+}/Fe^{2+}}^{\circ}=-3 \times F \times y-(-2 \times F \times x) \\ & E_{Fe^{3+}/Fe^{2+}}^{\circ}=3y-2x \end{aligned}$ Option (B) is correct

questions.question_text: An electrochemical cell is constructed using half cells in the direction of spontaneous change: Fe(OH) 2 (s) + 2e − → Fe(s) + 2OH − (aq)      E θ = −0.88 V and AgBr(s) + e − → Ag(s) + Br − (aq)      E θ = +0.07 V Which of the following option is correct ?
questions.question_html:
An electrochemical cell is constructed using half cells in the direction of spontaneous change:

Fe(OH)2(s) + 2e− → Fe(s) + 2OH−(aq)      Eθ = −0.88 V

and AgBr(s) + e− → Ag(s) + Br−(aq)      Eθ = +0.07 V

Which of the following option is correct?

options.label: A
options.html: $\text{Overall reaction}Fe(s)+2OH^{-}(aq)+2AgBr(s) \rightleftharpoons Fe(OH)_{2}(s)+2Ag(s)+2Br^{-}(aq)$

options.label: C
options.text: Fe is reduced in the electrochemical cell
options.html: Fe is reduced in the electrochemical cell

options.label: D
options.html: $E_{cell}^{\theta}$ is an extensive property

questions.explanation_text: For a spontaneous electrochemical cell, the half-reaction with higher standard reduction potential undergoes reduction, and the other one undergoes oxidation. Given half-reactions: $Fe(OH)_{2}(s)+2e^{-} \rightarrow Fe(s)+2OH^{-}(aq)E^{\theta}=-0.88\text{V}$ $AgBr(s)+e^{-} \rightarrow Ag(s)+Br^{-}(aq)E^{\theta}=+0.07\text{V}$ Since $+0.07\text{V}>-0.88\text{V}$ , the $AgBr/Ag$ half-cell will undergo reduction and the iron half-cell will undergo oxidation. So reverse the iron half-reaction: $Fe(s)+2OH^{-}(aq) \rightarrow Fe(OH)_{2}(s)+2e^{-}$ Multiply the silver half-reaction by $2$ : $2AgBr(s)+2e^{-} \rightarrow 2Ag(s)+2Br^{-}(aq)$ Now add them: $Fe(s)+2OH^{-}(aq)+2AgBr(s) \rightarrow Fe(OH)_{2}(s)+2Ag(s)+2Br^{-}(aq)$ This matches Option A. Now calculate $E_{\text{cell}}^{\theta}$ : $E_{\text{cell}}^{\theta}=E_{\text{cathode}}^{\theta}-E_{\text{anode}}^{\theta}$ Here, cathode: $AgBr/Ag$ , so $E_{\text{cathode}}^{\theta}=+0.07\text{V}$ anode: reduction potential of $Fe(OH)_{2}/Fe$ is $-0.88\text{V}$ Therefore, $E_{\text{cell}}^{\theta}=0.07-(-0.88)=0.95\text{V}$ So Option B is false. Option C is false because Fe is oxidised, not reduced. Option D is false because $E_{\text{cell}}^{\theta}$ is an intensive property, not an extensive property. Hence, the correct option is: $\text{Option A}$
questions.explanation_html:
For a spontaneous electrochemical cell, the half-reaction with higher standard reduction potential undergoes reduction, and the other one undergoes oxidation.

Given half-reactions:

$Fe(OH)_{2}(s)+2e^{-} \rightarrow Fe(s)+2OH^{-}(aq)E^{\theta}=-0.88\text{V}$

$AgBr(s)+e^{-} \rightarrow Ag(s)+Br^{-}(aq)E^{\theta}=+0.07\text{V}$

Since $+0.07\text{V}>-0.88\text{V}$ , the $AgBr/Ag$ half-cell will undergo reduction and the iron half-cell will undergo oxidation.

So reverse the iron half-reaction:

$Fe(s)+2OH^{-}(aq) \rightarrow Fe(OH)_{2}(s)+2e^{-}$

Multiply the silver half-reaction by $2$ :

$2AgBr(s)+2e^{-} \rightarrow 2Ag(s)+2Br^{-}(aq)$

Now add them:

$Fe(s)+2OH^{-}(aq)+2AgBr(s) \rightarrow Fe(OH)_{2}(s)+2Ag(s)+2Br^{-}(aq)$

This matches Option A.

Now calculate $E_{\text{cell}}^{\theta}$ :

$E_{\text{cell}}^{\theta}=E_{\text{cathode}}^{\theta}-E_{\text{anode}}^{\theta}$

Here,

  • cathode: $AgBr/Ag$ , so $E_{\text{cathode}}^{\theta}=+0.07\text{V}$

  • anode: reduction potential of $Fe(OH)_{2}/Fe$ is $-0.88\text{V}$

Therefore,

$E_{\text{cell}}^{\theta}=0.07-(-0.88)=0.95\text{V}$

So Option B is false.

Option C is false because Fe is oxidised, not reduced.

Option D is false because $E_{\text{cell}}^{\theta}$ is an intensive property, not an extensive property.

Hence, the correct option is:

$\text{Option A}$

questions.question_text: At 298 K , the molar conductivity of $x%(w/w)MX$ solution (aqueous) is $123.5Scm^{2}mol^{-1}$ . The conductance of same solution is $1.9 \times 10^{-3}S$ . The value of $x$ is $____$ $\times 10^{-2}$ . (Given: cell constant $=1.3cm^{-1}$ ; molar mass of MX is $75gmol^{-1}$ , density of aqueous solution of MX at 298 K is $1.0gmL^{-1}$ )
questions.question_html:
At 298 K , the molar conductivity of $x%(w/w)MX$ solution (aqueous) is $123.5Scm^{2}mol^{-1}$ . The conductance of same solution is $1.9 \times 10^{-3}S$ . The value of $x$ is $____$ $\times 10^{-2}$ .

(Given: cell constant $=1.3cm^{-1}$ ; molar mass of MX is $75gmol^{-1}$ , density of aqueous solution of MX at 298 K is $1.0gmL^{-1}$ )
questions.explanation_text: Conductivity ( $\kappa$ ) is related to the conductance ( $G$ ) and the cell constant ( $G^{∗}$ ) by the following relationship: $\kappa=G \times G^{∗}$ Substituting the given values: $\kappa=(1.9 \times 10^{-3}S) \times (1.3cm^{-1})$ $\kappa=2.47 \times 10^{-3}Scm^{-1}$ The molar conductivity ( $\Lambda_{m}$ ) is related to the conductivity ( $\kappa$ ) and the molarity ( $C$ in $molL^{-1}$ ) by the formula: $\Lambda_{m}=\frac{\kappa \times 1000}{C}$ Rearranging the formula to solve for molarity ( $C$ ): $C=\frac{\kappa \times 1000}{\Lambda_{m}}$ Substituting the values into the equation: $C=\frac{(2.47 \times 10^{-3}Scm^{-1}) \times 1000cm^{3}L^{-1}}{123.5Scm^{2}mol^{-1}}$ $C=\frac{2.47}{123.5}molL^{-1}$ $C=0.02molL^{-1}$ An $x%(w/w)$ aqueous solution means there are $xg$ of the solute (MX) in $100g$ of the solution. Using the density of the solution, we can find the volume of $100g$ of the solution: $\text{Volume of solution}=\frac{\text{Mass of solution}}{\text{Density}}$ $\text{Volume}=\frac{100g}{1.0gmL^{-1}}=100mL$ Molarity is defined as the number of moles of solute per $1000mL$ (1 liter) of the solution. Since $100mL$ of the solution contains $xg$ of MX, $1000mL$ of the solution will contain $10xg$ of MX. Now, calculate the number of moles of MX in $1000mL$ , which is exactly our molarity ( $C$ ): $\text{Moles in 1 L}=\frac{\text{Mass of solute in 1 L}}{\text{Molar mass of solute}}$ $C=\frac{10x}{75}$ We already calculated the molarity to be $0.02molL^{-1}$ . Equating the two values: $\frac{10x}{75}=0.02$ $10x=0.02 \times 75$ $10x=1.5$ $x=0.15$ The problem requires $x$ to be expressed in the form of $____ \times 10^{-2}$ . $x=0.15=15 \times 10^{-2}$ The value of $x$ is 15.
questions.explanation_html:
Conductivity ( $\kappa$ ) is related to the conductance ( $G$ ) and the cell constant ( $G^{∗}$ ) by the following relationship:

$\kappa=G \times G^{∗}$

Substituting the given values:

$\kappa=(1.9 \times 10^{-3}S) \times (1.3cm^{-1})$

$\kappa=2.47 \times 10^{-3}Scm^{-1}$

The molar conductivity ( $\Lambda_{m}$ ) is related to the conductivity ( $\kappa$ ) and the molarity ( $C$ in $molL^{-1}$ ) by the formula:

$\Lambda_{m}=\frac{\kappa \times 1000}{C}$

Rearranging the formula to solve for molarity ( $C$ ):

$C=\frac{\kappa \times 1000}{\Lambda_{m}}$

Substituting the values into the equation:

$C=\frac{(2.47 \times 10^{-3}Scm^{-1}) \times 1000cm^{3}L^{-1}}{123.5Scm^{2}mol^{-1}}$

$C=\frac{2.47}{123.5}molL^{-1}$

$C=0.02molL^{-1}$

An $x%(w/w)$ aqueous solution means there are $xg$ of the solute (MX) in $100g$ of the solution.

Using the density of the solution, we can find the volume of $100g$ of the solution:

$\text{Volume of solution}=\frac{\text{Mass of solution}}{\text{Density}}$

$\text{Volume}=\frac{100g}{1.0gmL^{-1}}=100mL$

Molarity is defined as the number of moles of solute per $1000mL$ (1 liter) of the solution.

Since $100mL$ of the solution contains $xg$ of MX, $1000mL$ of the solution will contain $10xg$ of MX.

Now, calculate the number of moles of MX in $1000mL$ , which is exactly our molarity ( $C$ ):

$\text{Moles in 1 L}=\frac{\text{Mass of solute in 1 L}}{\text{Molar mass of solute}}$

$C=\frac{10x}{75}$

We already calculated the molarity to be $0.02molL^{-1}$ . Equating the two values:

$\frac{10x}{75}=0.02$

$10x=0.02 \times 75$

$10x=1.5$

$x=0.15$

The problem requires $x$ to be expressed in the form of $____ \times 10^{-2}$ .

$x=0.15=15 \times 10^{-2}$

The value of $x$ is 15.

questions.question_text: For strong electrolyte $\Lambda_{m}$ increases slowly with dilution and can be represented by the equation $\Lambda_{m}=\Lambda_{m}^{\circ}-Ac^{1/2}$ Molar conductivity values of the solutions of strong electrolyte AB at 18°C are given below : c [mol L -1 ] 0.04 0.09 0.16 0.25 $\Lambda_{m}$ [S cm 2 mol -1 ] 96.1 95.7 95.3 94.9 The value of constant A based on the above data [in S cm 2 mol -1 /(mol/L) 1/2 ] unit is ________.
questions.question_html:
For strong electrolyte $\Lambda_{m}$ increases slowly with dilution and can be represented by the equation

$\Lambda_{m}=\Lambda_{m}^{\circ}-Ac^{1/2}$

Molar conductivity values of the solutions of strong electrolyte AB at 18°C are given below :

c [mol L-1]0.040.090.160.25
$\Lambda_{m}$ [S cm2 mol-1]96.195.795.394.9

The value of constant A based on the above data [in S cm2 mol-1/(mol/L)1/2] unit is ________.
questions.explanation_text: We use the given relation for a strong electrolyte: Using equation : $\Lambda_{m}=\Lambda_{m}^{0}-A\sqrt{c}$ Now substitute the first set of data: $c=0.04$ and $\Lambda_{m}=96.1$ . $\begin{aligned} & 96.1=\Lambda_{m}^{0}-A\sqrt{0.04} \\ & 96.1=\Lambda_{m}^{0}-A \times 0.2...(i) \\ & 95.7=\Lambda_{m}^{0}-A \times \sqrt{0.09} \\ & 95.7=\Lambda_{m}^{0}-A \times 0.3...(ii) \end{aligned}$ Now subtract equation (ii) from equation (i) so that $\Lambda_{m}^{0}$ cancels out: From eq. (1) and eq. (2) $\begin{aligned} (96.1-95.7) & =(\Lambda_{m}^{0}-A \times 0.2)-(\Lambda_{m}^{0}-A \times 0.3) \\ 0.4 & =-0.2A+0.3A \\ 0.4 & =0.1A \\ A & =4 \end{aligned}$
questions.explanation_html:
We use the given relation for a strong electrolyte:

Using equation : $\Lambda_{m}=\Lambda_{m}^{0}-A\sqrt{c}$

Now substitute the first set of data: $c=0.04$ and $\Lambda_{m}=96.1$ .

$\begin{aligned} & 96.1=\Lambda_{m}^{0}-A\sqrt{0.04} \\ & 96.1=\Lambda_{m}^{0}-A \times 0.2...(i) \\ & 95.7=\Lambda_{m}^{0}-A \times \sqrt{0.09} \\ & 95.7=\Lambda_{m}^{0}-A \times 0.3...(ii) \end{aligned}$

Now subtract equation (ii) from equation (i) so that $\Lambda_{m}^{0}$ cancels out:

From eq. (1) and eq. (2)

$\begin{aligned} (96.1-95.7) & =(\Lambda_{m}^{0}-A \times 0.2)-(\Lambda_{m}^{0}-A \times 0.3) \\ 0.4 & =-0.2A+0.3A \\ 0.4 & =0.1A \\ A & =4 \end{aligned}$

questions.question_text: Consider the following electrochemical cell : $Pt|O_{2}(g)(1bar)|HCl(aq)‖M^{2+}(aq,1.0M)|M(s)$ The pH above which, oxygen gas would start to evolve at anode is $____$ (nearest integer). $[\begin{aligned} \text{Given :} & E_{M^{2+}/M}^{o}=0.994V \\ & E_{O_{2}/H_{2}O}^{o}=1.23V \end{aligned}}\text{standard reduction potential}\text{and}\frac{RT}{F}(2.303)=0.059V\text{at the given condition}]$
questions.question_html:
Consider the following electrochemical cell :

$Pt|O_{2}(g)(1bar)|HCl(aq)‖M^{2+}(aq,1.0M)|M(s)$

The pH above which, oxygen gas would start to evolve at anode is $____$ (nearest integer).

$[\begin{aligned} \text{Given :} & E_{M^{2+}/M}^{o}=0.994V \\ & E_{O_{2}/H_{2}O}^{o}=1.23V \end{aligned}}\text{standard reduction potential}\text{and}\frac{RT}{F}(2.303)=0.059V\text{at the given condition}]$
questions.explanation_text: For the oxygen electrode (reduction reaction): $O_{2}(g)+4H^{+}(aq)+4e^{-} \rightarrow 2H_{2}O(l)$ Nernst equation: $E_{O_{2}/H_{2}O}=E_{O_{2}/H_{2}O}^{\circ}-\frac{0.059}{4}log(\frac{1}{p_{O_{2}}[H^{+}]^{4}})$ Given $p_{O_{2}}=1$ bar, so $logp_{O_{2}}=0$ : $E_{O_{2}/H_{2}O}=1.23+0.059log[H^{+}]$ Since $log[H^{+}]=-pH$ : $E_{O_{2}/H_{2}O}=1.23-0.059pH$ For the metal electrode: $M^{2+}+2e^{-} \rightarrow M(s)$ Given $[M^{2+}]=1.0M$ , hence $E_{M^{2+}/M}=E_{M^{2+}/M}^{\circ}=0.994V$ Oxygen will start evolving at the anode when the oxygen electrode becomes the anode , i.e. when its reduction potential becomes less than that of $M^{2+}/M$ . The threshold is when both are equal: $1.23-0.059pH=0.994$ $0.059pH=1.23-0.994=0.236$ $pH=\frac{0.236}{0.059}=4$ So, oxygen gas starts evolving at the anode for $pH>4$ . $4$
questions.explanation_html:
For the oxygen electrode (reduction reaction):

$O_{2}(g)+4H^{+}(aq)+4e^{-} \rightarrow 2H_{2}O(l)$

Nernst equation:

$E_{O_{2}/H_{2}O}=E_{O_{2}/H_{2}O}^{\circ}-\frac{0.059}{4}log(\frac{1}{p_{O_{2}}[H^{+}]^{4}})$

Given $p_{O_{2}}=1$ bar, so $logp_{O_{2}}=0$ :

$E_{O_{2}/H_{2}O}=1.23+0.059log[H^{+}]$

Since $log[H^{+}]=-pH$ :

$E_{O_{2}/H_{2}O}=1.23-0.059pH$

For the metal electrode:

$M^{2+}+2e^{-} \rightarrow M(s)$

Given $[M^{2+}]=1.0M$ , hence

$E_{M^{2+}/M}=E_{M^{2+}/M}^{\circ}=0.994V$

Oxygen will start evolving at the anode when the oxygen electrode becomes the anode, i.e. when its reduction potential becomes less than that of $M^{2+}/M$ . The threshold is when both are equal:

$1.23-0.059pH=0.994$

$0.059pH=1.23-0.994=0.236$

$pH=\frac{0.236}{0.059}=4$

So, oxygen gas starts evolving at the anode for $pH>4$ .

$4$

questions.question_text: For a general redox reaction Anode $Red_{1} \rightarrow Ox_{1}^{n_{1}^{+}}+n_{1}e^{-}$ Cathode $Ox_{2}+n_{2}e^{-} \rightarrow Red_{2}^{n_{2}-}$ Which of the following statement is incorrect?
questions.question_html:
For a general redox reaction

Anode $Red_{1} \rightarrow Ox_{1}^{n_{1}^{+}}+n_{1}e^{-}$

Cathode $Ox_{2}+n_{2}e^{-} \rightarrow Red_{2}^{n_{2}-}$

Which of the following statement is incorrect?

options.label: A
options.text: $\begin{aligned} & \text{The overall reaction can be written as}n_{2}Red_{1}+n_{1}Ox_{2} \rightleftharpoons n_{2}Ox_{1}^{n_{1}^{+}}+n_{1}Red_{2}^{n_{2}^{-}} \\ & \end{aligned}$
options.html: $\begin{aligned} & \text{The overall reaction can be written as}n_{2}Red_{1}+n_{1}Ox_{2} \rightleftharpoons n_{2}Ox_{1}^{n_{1}^{+}}+n_{1}Red_{2}^{n_{2}^{-}} \\ & \end{aligned}$

options.label: B
options.text: The electrons do not appear in the overall reaction because electrons produced at the anode are consumed at the cathode.
options.html: The electrons do not appear in the overall reaction because electrons produced at the anode are consumed at the cathode.

options.label: C
options.text: Here $n$ is the number of electrons transferred in redox reaction.
options.html: Here $n$ is the number of electrons transferred in redox reaction.

options.label: D
options.text: If the reaction is carried out reversibly, the electrical work done is equal to the ratio of charge and potential difference through which charge is moved.
options.html: If the reaction is carried out reversibly, the electrical work done is equal to the ratio of charge and potential difference through which charge is moved.

questions.explanation_text: $\begin{aligned} & \\ & \begin{aligned} (a)Anode: & (Red1 \longrightarrow O_{x_{1}}^{n^{+}}+u_{1}e^{-}) \cdot n_{2} \\ & (Ox_{2}+n_{2}e^{-} \longrightarrow Red_{2}^{n_{2}^{-}}) \cdot n_{1} \end{aligned} \end{aligned}$ To add the anode and cathode half-reactions, the number of electrons must be the same on both sides. So, we multiply the anode reaction by $n_{2}$ and the cathode reaction by $n_{1}$ , so that both have $n_{1}n_{2}$ electrons. $\begin{aligned} & \begin{aligned} & n_{2}Red_{1} \longrightarrow n_{2}Ox_{1}^{n+}+n_{2}n_{1}e^{-} \\ & n_{1}Ox_{2}+n_{1}n_{2}e^{-} \longrightarrow n_{1}Red_{2}^{n_{2}-} \end{aligned} \\ & \text{Overall ren:}n_{2}Red+n_{1}Ox_{2} \longrightarrow n_{2}Ox^{n+}+n_{1}Red_{2}^{n_{2}-} \end{aligned}$ Now, when we add these two equations, the $n_{1}n_{2}e^{-}$ on the product side of the anode reaction cancels with the $n_{1}n_{2}e^{-}$ on the reactant side of the cathode reaction. (b) The $e^{-}$ produced at the anode are consumed at the cathode, that's why $e^{-}$ do not appear in the overall reaction. This statement is correct because electrons cancel during addition of the two half-reactions. (c) We know, $\begin{aligned} & E=E^{o}-\frac{RT}{nf}logQ \\ & E-E^{\circ}=\frac{-RT}{nf}logQ \\ & \frac{E-E^{\circ}}{RT/f}=-\frac{1}{n}logQ \end{aligned}$ Here, $E$ changes with $logQ$ according to the Nernst equation, and $n$ is the number of electrons transferred in the balanced redox reaction. plotting a $y=mx+c$ graph, $\begin{aligned} & y=\frac{E-E^{0}}{RT/F} \\ & x=logQ \\ & \text{slope}(m)=-\frac{1}{n} \\ & \text{slope}∝\frac{1}{n} \end{aligned}$ So, the slope is $-\frac{1}{n}$ . This statement is also correct. $\text{Where,}n=\text{no. of}e^{-}\text{transfered in redox reaction.}$ (D) The electrical work done by a galvanic cell is given by the product of the total charge transfered and the potential difference, not their ratio. This statement is correct because electrical work is given by $W=qV$ (charge multiplied by potential difference). $\begin{aligned} W_{electrical} & =\text{charge × Potential difference.} \\ & =Q \times V \end{aligned}$ $W_{e}=It \times V$
questions.explanation_html:
$\begin{aligned} & \\ & \begin{aligned} (a)Anode: & (Red1 \longrightarrow O_{x_{1}}^{n^{+}}+u_{1}e^{-}) \cdot n_{2} \\ & (Ox_{2}+n_{2}e^{-} \longrightarrow Red_{2}^{n_{2}^{-}}) \cdot n_{1} \end{aligned} \end{aligned}$

To add the anode and cathode half-reactions, the number of electrons must be the same on both sides.

So, we multiply the anode reaction by $n_{2}$ and the cathode reaction by $n_{1}$ , so that both have $n_{1}n_{2}$ electrons.

$\begin{aligned} & \begin{aligned} & n_{2}Red_{1} \longrightarrow n_{2}Ox_{1}^{n+}+n_{2}n_{1}e^{-} \\ & n_{1}Ox_{2}+n_{1}n_{2}e^{-} \longrightarrow n_{1}Red_{2}^{n_{2}-} \end{aligned} \\ & \text{Overall ren:}n_{2}Red+n_{1}Ox_{2} \longrightarrow n_{2}Ox^{n+}+n_{1}Red_{2}^{n_{2}-} \end{aligned}$

Now, when we add these two equations, the $n_{1}n_{2}e^{-}$ on the product side of the anode reaction cancels with the $n_{1}n_{2}e^{-}$ on the reactant side of the cathode reaction.

(b) The $e^{-}$ produced at the anode are consumed at the cathode, that's why $e^{-}$ do not appear in the overall reaction.

This statement is correct because electrons cancel during addition of the two half-reactions.

(c) We know,

$\begin{aligned} & E=E^{o}-\frac{RT}{nf}logQ \\ & E-E^{\circ}=\frac{-RT}{nf}logQ \\ & \frac{E-E^{\circ}}{RT/f}=-\frac{1}{n}logQ \end{aligned}$

Here, $E$ changes with $logQ$ according to the Nernst equation, and $n$ is the number of electrons transferred in the balanced redox reaction.

plotting a $y=mx+c$ graph,

$\begin{aligned} & y=\frac{E-E^{0}}{RT/F} \\ & x=logQ \\ & \text{slope}(m)=-\frac{1}{n} \\ & \text{slope}∝\frac{1}{n} \end{aligned}$

So, the slope is $-\frac{1}{n}$ . This statement is also correct.

$\text{Where,}n=\text{no. of}e^{-}\text{transfered in redox reaction.}$

(D) The electrical work done by a galvanic cell is given by the product of the total charge transfered and the potential difference, not their ratio.

This statement is correct because electrical work is given by $W=qV$ (charge multiplied by potential difference).

$\begin{aligned} W_{electrical} & =\text{charge × Potential difference.} \\ & =Q \times V \end{aligned}$

                 $W_{e}=It \times V$

questions.question_text: Consider the above electrochemical cell where a metal electrode ( M ) is undergoing redox reaction by forming $M^{+}(M \rightarrow M^{+}+e^{-})$ . The cation $M^{+}$ is present in two different concentrations $c_{1}$ and $c_{2}$ as shown above. Which of the following statement is correct for generating a positive cell potential?
questions.question_html: Consider the above electrochemical cell where a metal electrode ( M ) is undergoing redox reaction by forming $M^{+}(M \rightarrow M^{+}+e^{-})$ . The cation $M^{+}$ is present in two different concentrations $c_{1}$ and $c_{2}$ as shown above. Which of the following statement is correct for generating a positive cell potential?

options.label: A
options.text: If $c_{1}$ is present at anode, then $c_{1}>c_{2}$ .
options.html: If $c_{1}$ is present at anode, then $c_{1}>c_{2}$ .

options.label: B

options.html: If $c_{1}$ is present at cathode, then $c_{1}>c_{2}$ .

questions.explanation_text: (1) If $C_{1}$ is at anode ⇒ cell reaction $\begin{aligned} & M^{+}(C_{2}) \rightarrow M^{+}(C_{1}) \\ & E_{\text{cell}}=-0.059log\frac{C_{1}}{C_{2}} \\ & \therefore E_{\text{cell}}>0 \Rightarrow C_{1}<C_{2} \end{aligned}$ (2) If $C_{1}$ is at cathode $\begin{aligned} & M^{+}(C_{1}) \rightarrow M^{+}(C_{2}) \\ & E_{\text{cell}}=-0.059log\frac{C_{2}}{C_{1}}>0 \\ & C_{2}<C_{1} \end{aligned}$
questions.explanation_html:
(1) If $C_{1}$ is at anode ⇒ cell reaction

$\begin{aligned} & M^{+}(C_{2}) \rightarrow M^{+}(C_{1}) \\ & E_{\text{cell}}=-0.059log\frac{C_{1}}{C_{2}} \\ & \therefore E_{\text{cell}}>0 \Rightarrow C_{1}<C_{2} \end{aligned}$

(2) If $C_{1}$ is at cathode

questions.explanation_text: For the cell, the two reduction potentials are: $M^{x+}+xe^{-} \rightarrow M(s),E_{\text{red}}^{\circ}=+0.15\text{V}$ and $Fe^{3+}+3e^{-} \rightarrow Fe(s),E_{\text{red}}^{\circ}=-0.036\text{V}$ Since the reduction potential of $M^{x+}/M$ is greater, it will act as the cathode. So, Cathode: $M^{x+}+xe^{-} \rightarrow M(s)$ Anode: $Fe(s) \rightarrow Fe^{3+}+3e^{-}$ Hence, $E_{\text{cell}}^{\circ}=E_{\text{cathode}}^{\circ}-E_{\text{anode}}^{\circ}=0.15-(-0.036)=0.186\text{V}$ Now use the Nernst equation: $E_{\text{cell}}=E_{\text{cell}}^{\circ}-\frac{0.059}{n}logQ$ Given: $E_{\text{cell}}=0.2057\text{V},Q=10^{-2}$ Since $log10^{-2}=-2$ , $0.2057=0.186-\frac{0.059}{n}(-2)$ $0.2057=0.186+\frac{0.118}{n}$ $0.2057-0.186=\frac{0.118}{n}$ $0.0197=\frac{0.118}{n}$ $n=\frac{0.118}{0.0197} \approx 5.99 \approx 6$ So the number of electrons transferred in the balanced cell reaction is $n=6$ Now, for balancing electrons: Oxidation of iron gives $3$ electrons Reduction of $M^{x+}$ consumes $x$ electrons Therefore, total electrons transferred in the balanced equation will be $LCM(3,x)$ . Given this is $6$ , we get: $LCM(3,x)=6$ Possible values of $x$ are $2$ or $6$ . Now it is given that $M$ is a p-block metal. Common p-block metals generally form ions like $2^{+}$ , $3^{+}$ , $4^{+}$ , etc. Among the possible values, the most suitable is $x=2$ So, the nearest integer value of $x$ is $2$
questions.explanation_html:
For the cell, the two reduction potentials are:

$M^{x+}+xe^{-} \rightarrow M(s),E_{\text{red}}^{\circ}=+0.15\text{V}$

and

$Fe^{3+}+3e^{-} \rightarrow Fe(s),E_{\text{red}}^{\circ}=-0.036\text{V}$

Since the reduction potential of $M^{x+}/M$ is greater, it will act as the cathode.

So,

  • Cathode: $M^{x+}+xe^{-} \rightarrow M(s)$

  • Anode: $Fe(s) \rightarrow Fe^{3+}+3e^{-}$

Hence,

$E_{\text{cell}}^{\circ}=E_{\text{cathode}}^{\circ}-E_{\text{anode}}^{\circ}=0.15-(-0.036)=0.186\text{V}$

Now use the Nernst equation:

$E_{\text{cell}}=E_{\text{cell}}^{\circ}-\frac{0.059}{n}logQ$

Given:

$E_{\text{cell}}=0.2057\text{V},Q=10^{-2}$

Since $log10^{-2}=-2$ ,

$0.2057=0.186-\frac{0.059}{n}(-2)$

$0.2057=0.186+\frac{0.118}{n}$

$0.2057-0.186=\frac{0.118}{n}$

$0.0197=\frac{0.118}{n}$

$n=\frac{0.118}{0.0197} \approx 5.99 \approx 6$

So the number of electrons transferred in the balanced cell reaction is

$n=6$

Now, for balancing electrons:

  • Oxidation of iron gives $3$ electrons

  • Reduction of $M^{x+}$ consumes $x$ electrons

Therefore, total electrons transferred in the balanced equation will be $LCM(3,x)$ .

Given this is $6$ , we get:

$LCM(3,x)=6$

Possible values of $x$ are $2$ or $6$ .

Now it is given that $M$ is a p-block metal. Common p-block metals generally form ions like $2^{+}$ , $3^{+}$ , $4^{+}$ , etc. Among the possible values, the most suitable is

$x=2$

So, the nearest integer value of $x$ is

$2$

questions.question_html:
Consider the following redox reaction taking place in acidic medium

$BH_{4}^{-}(aq)+ClO_{3}^{-}(aq) \longrightarrow H_{2}BO_{3}^{-}(aq)+Cl^{-}(aq)$

If the Nernst equation for the above balanced reaction is

$E_{cell}=E_{cell}^{\circ}-\frac{RT}{nF}lnQ,$

then the value of $n$ is $____$ .(Nearest integer)
questions.explanation_text: Balance by ion–electron method in acidic medium. Oxidation half-reaction (borohydride to dihydrogen borate): Start: $BH_{4}^{-} \rightarrow H_{2}BO_{3}^{-}$ Balance O by adding water: $BH_{4}^{-}+3H_{2}O \rightarrow H_{2}BO_{3}^{-}$ Balance H by adding $H^{+}$ : Left H = $4+6=10$ , right H = $2$ , so add $8H^{+}$ on RHS: $BH_{4}^{-}+3H_{2}O \rightarrow H_{2}BO_{3}^{-}+8H^{+}$ Balance charge by adding electrons (oxidation ⇒ $e^{-}$ on RHS): LHS charge $=-1$ , RHS charge $=-1+8=+7$ , so add $8e^{-}$ to RHS: $BH_{4}^{-}+3H_{2}O \rightarrow H_{2}BO_{3}^{-}+8H^{+}+8e^{-}$ So, electrons lost $=8$ . Reduction half-reaction (chlorate to chloride): $ClO_{3}^{-} \rightarrow Cl^{-}$ Balance O by adding water: $ClO_{3}^{-} \rightarrow Cl^{-}+3H_{2}O$ Balance H by adding $H^{+}$ on LHS: $6H^{+}+ClO_{3}^{-} \rightarrow Cl^{-}+3H_{2}O$ Balance charge by adding electrons (reduction ⇒ $e^{-}$ on LHS): LHS charge $=6-1=+5$ , RHS charge $=-1$ , so add $6e^{-}$ to LHS: $6e^{-}+6H^{+}+ClO_{3}^{-} \rightarrow Cl^{-}+3H_{2}O$ So, electrons gained $=6$ . Make electrons equal (LCM of $8$ and $6$ is $24$ ): Multiply oxidation half by $3$ and reduction half by $4$ : Oxidation $\times 3$ gives $24e^{-}$ , reduction $\times 4$ consumes $24e^{-}$ . After adding and canceling common species, the balanced overall reaction becomes: $3BH_{4}^{-}+4ClO_{3}^{-} \rightarrow 3H_{2}BO_{3}^{-}+4Cl^{-}+3H_{2}O$ Hence, the number of electrons transferred in the balanced reaction is $n=24.$ So, $n=24$ (nearest integer).
questions.explanation_html:
Balance by ion–electron method in acidic medium.

Oxidation half-reaction (borohydride to dihydrogen borate):

Start: $BH_{4}^{-} \rightarrow H_{2}BO_{3}^{-}$

Balance O by adding water:

$BH_{4}^{-}+3H_{2}O \rightarrow H_{2}BO_{3}^{-}$

Balance H by adding $H^{+}$ :

Left H = $4+6=10$ , right H = $2$ , so add $8H^{+}$ on RHS:

$BH_{4}^{-}+3H_{2}O \rightarrow H_{2}BO_{3}^{-}+8H^{+}$

Balance charge by adding electrons (oxidation ⇒ $e^{-}$ on RHS):

LHS charge $=-1$ , RHS charge $=-1+8=+7$ , so add $8e^{-}$ to RHS:

$BH_{4}^{-}+3H_{2}O \rightarrow H_{2}BO_{3}^{-}+8H^{+}+8e^{-}$

So, electrons lost $=8$ .

Reduction half-reaction (chlorate to chloride):

$ClO_{3}^{-} \rightarrow Cl^{-}$

Balance O by adding water:

$ClO_{3}^{-} \rightarrow Cl^{-}+3H_{2}O$

Balance H by adding $H^{+}$ on LHS:

$6H^{+}+ClO_{3}^{-} \rightarrow Cl^{-}+3H_{2}O$

Balance charge by adding electrons (reduction ⇒ $e^{-}$ on LHS):

LHS charge $=6-1=+5$ , RHS charge $=-1$ , so add $6e^{-}$ to LHS:

$6e^{-}+6H^{+}+ClO_{3}^{-} \rightarrow Cl^{-}+3H_{2}O$

So, electrons gained $=6$ .

Make electrons equal (LCM of $8$ and $6$ is $24$ ):

Multiply oxidation half by $3$ and reduction half by $4$ :

Oxidation $\times 3$ gives $24e^{-}$ , reduction $\times 4$ consumes $24e^{-}$ .

After adding and canceling common species, the balanced overall reaction becomes:

$3BH_{4}^{-}+4ClO_{3}^{-} \rightarrow 3H_{2}BO_{3}^{-}+4Cl^{-}+3H_{2}O$

Hence, the number of electrons transferred in the balanced reaction is

$n=24.$

So, $n=24$ (nearest integer).

If the conductivity of the saturated $BaSO_{4}$ solution is $xScm^{-1}$ then the solubility product of $BaSO_{4}$ can be given as (Here $\wedge_{m}=\wedge_{m}^{\circ}$ )
questions.question_html:
$\text{Consider the following data.}$

$\begin{aligned} \text{Electrolyte} & \wedge_{m}^{\circ}(Scm^{𝟐}mol^{𝟏}) \\ BaCl_{2} & x_{1} \\ H_{2}SO_{4} & x_{2} \\ HCl & x_{3} \end{aligned}$

$BaSO_{4}$ is sparingly soluble in water. If the conductivity of the saturated $BaSO_{4}$ solution is $xScm^{-1}$ then the solubility product of $BaSO_{4}$ can be given as (Here $\wedge_{m}=\wedge_{m}^{\circ}$ )
questions.explanation_text: $BaSO_{4}(s) \rightleftharpoons Ba^{2+}(aq)+SO_{4}^{2-}(aq)$ If the solubility of $BaSO_{4}$ is $s\text{mol L}^{-1}$ , then in solution: $[Ba^{2+}]=s,[SO_{4}^{2-}]=s$ Thus, the solubility product is $K_{\text{sp}}=[Ba^{2+}][SO_{4}^{2-}]=s^{2}$ Relation between molar conductivity and observed conductivity By definition, $\kappa=\frac{\Lambda_{m}c}{1000}$ where $\kappa$ = conductivity in $\text{S cm}^{-1}$ , $\Lambda_{m}$ = molar conductivity in $\text{S cm}^{2}\text{mol}^{-1}$ , $c$ = molar concentration in $\text{mol L}^{-1}$ . For the saturated solution of $BaSO_{4}$ , $\kappa=x$ and $c=s$ Therefore, $\Lambda_{m}^{\text{(BaSO}_{4})}=\frac{1000x}{s}$ Determining $\Lambda_{m}^{\circ}$ for $BaSO_{4}$ We can find $\Lambda_{m}^{\circ}$ for $BaSO_{4}$ using Kohlrausch’s law of independent migration of ions . According to the law, $\Lambda_{m}^{\circ}(\text{Electrolyte})=\text{sum of molar ionic conductivities of its ions}.$ Now, from the data: $\begin{aligned} \Lambda_{m}^{\circ}(BaCl_{2}) & =\lambda_{Ba^{2+}}^{\circ}+2\lambda_{Cl^{-}}^{\circ}=x_{1} \\ \Lambda_{m}^{\circ}(H_{2}SO_{4}) & =2\lambda_{H^{+}}^{\circ}+\lambda_{SO_{4}^{2-}}^{\circ}=x_{2} \\ \Lambda_{m}^{\circ}(HCl) & =\lambda_{H^{+}}^{\circ}+\lambda_{Cl^{-}}^{\circ}=x_{3} \end{aligned}$ To get $\Lambda_{m}^{\circ}(BaSO_{4})=\lambda_{Ba^{2+}}^{\circ}+\lambda_{SO_{4}^{2-}}^{\circ}$ , we combine the above equations: $(x_{1}+x_{2}-2x_{3})=(\lambda_{Ba^{2+}}^{\circ}+2\lambda_{Cl^{-}}^{\circ})+(2\lambda_{H^{+}}^{\circ}+\lambda_{SO_{4}^{2-}}^{\circ})-2(\lambda_{H^{+}}^{\circ}+\lambda_{Cl^{-}}^{\circ})$ Simplifying, $x_{1}+x_{2}-2x_{3}=\lambda_{Ba^{2+}}^{\circ}+\lambda_{SO_{4}^{2-}}^{\circ}=\Lambda_{m}^{\circ}(BaSO_{4})$ Thus, $\Lambda_{m}^{\circ}(BaSO_{4})=x_{1}+x_{2}-2x_{3}$ Equating conductivities Since it is given that $(\Lambda_{m}=\Lambda_{m}^{\circ})$ for the saturated solution: $\Lambda_{m}^{\circ}=\frac{1000x}{s}$ $s=\frac{1000x}{\Lambda_{m}^{\circ}}=\frac{1000x}{x_{1}+x_{2}-2x_{3}}$ Expression for solubility product $K_{\text{sp}}=s^{2}=(\frac{1000x}{x_{1}+x_{2}-2x_{3}})^{2}=\frac{10^{6}x^{2}}{(x_{1}+x_{2}-2x_{3})^{2}}$ Final Answer $K_{\text{sp}}=\frac{10^{6}x^{2}}{(x_{1}+x_{2}-2x_{3})^{2}}$ Hence, Option A is correct.
questions.explanation_html:
$BaSO_{4}(s) \rightleftharpoons Ba^{2+}(aq)+SO_{4}^{2-}(aq)$

If the solubility of $BaSO_{4}$ is $s\text{mol L}^{-1}$ , then in solution:

$[Ba^{2+}]=s,[SO_{4}^{2-}]=s$

Thus, the solubility product is

$K_{\text{sp}}=[Ba^{2+}][SO_{4}^{2-}]=s^{2}$

Relation between molar conductivity and observed conductivity

By definition,

$\kappa=\frac{\Lambda_{m}c}{1000}$

where

  • $\kappa$ = conductivity in $\text{S cm}^{-1}$ ,

  • $\Lambda_{m}$ = molar conductivity in $\text{S cm}^{2}\text{mol}^{-1}$ ,

  • $c$ = molar concentration in $\text{mol L}^{-1}$ .

For the saturated solution of $BaSO_{4}$ ,

$\kappa=x$

and

$c=s$

Therefore,

$\Lambda_{m}^{\text{(BaSO}_{4})}=\frac{1000x}{s}$

Determining $\Lambda_{m}^{\circ}$ for $BaSO_{4}$

We can find $\Lambda_{m}^{\circ}$ for $BaSO_{4}$ using Kohlrausch’s law of independent migration of ions.

According to the law,

$\Lambda_{m}^{\circ}(\text{Electrolyte})=\text{sum of molar ionic conductivities of its ions}.$

Now, from the data:

$\begin{aligned} \Lambda_{m}^{\circ}(BaCl_{2}) & =\lambda_{Ba^{2+}}^{\circ}+2\lambda_{Cl^{-}}^{\circ}=x_{1} \\ \Lambda_{m}^{\circ}(H_{2}SO_{4}) & =2\lambda_{H^{+}}^{\circ}+\lambda_{SO_{4}^{2-}}^{\circ}=x_{2} \\ \Lambda_{m}^{\circ}(HCl) & =\lambda_{H^{+}}^{\circ}+\lambda_{Cl^{-}}^{\circ}=x_{3} \end{aligned}$

To get $\Lambda_{m}^{\circ}(BaSO_{4})=\lambda_{Ba^{2+}}^{\circ}+\lambda_{SO_{4}^{2-}}^{\circ}$ ,

we combine the above equations:

$(x_{1}+x_{2}-2x_{3})=(\lambda_{Ba^{2+}}^{\circ}+2\lambda_{Cl^{-}}^{\circ})+(2\lambda_{H^{+}}^{\circ}+\lambda_{SO_{4}^{2-}}^{\circ})-2(\lambda_{H^{+}}^{\circ}+\lambda_{Cl^{-}}^{\circ})$

Simplifying,

$x_{1}+x_{2}-2x_{3}=\lambda_{Ba^{2+}}^{\circ}+\lambda_{SO_{4}^{2-}}^{\circ}=\Lambda_{m}^{\circ}(BaSO_{4})$

Thus,

$\Lambda_{m}^{\circ}(BaSO_{4})=x_{1}+x_{2}-2x_{3}$

Equating conductivities

Since it is given that $(\Lambda_{m}=\Lambda_{m}^{\circ})$ for the saturated solution:

$\Lambda_{m}^{\circ}=\frac{1000x}{s}$

$s=\frac{1000x}{\Lambda_{m}^{\circ}}=\frac{1000x}{x_{1}+x_{2}-2x_{3}}$

Expression for solubility product

$K_{\text{sp}}=s^{2}=(\frac{1000x}{x_{1}+x_{2}-2x_{3}})^{2}=\frac{10^{6}x^{2}}{(x_{1}+x_{2}-2x_{3})^{2}}$

Final Answer

$K_{\text{sp}}=\frac{10^{6}x^{2}}{(x_{1}+x_{2}-2x_{3})^{2}}$

Hence, Option A is correct.

The fuel cell works with 80% efficiency. Consider the following two half-cell reactions along with the standard reduction potential given :

$CO_{2}+6H^{+}+6e^{-} \longrightarrow CH_{3}OH+H_{2}OE_{\text{red}}^{\circ}=0.02V$

$\frac{1}{2}O_{2}+2H^{+}+2e^{-} \longrightarrow H_{2}OE_{\text{red}}^{\circ}=1.23V$

If the work derived from the cell using 1 mol of $CH_{3}OH$ is used to compress an ideal gas isothermally against a constant pressure of 1 kPa, then the change in the volume of the gas,

$\Delta V=\underset{-}{}$ m $^{3}$ . (nearest integer)

Given : $F=96500Cmol^{-1}$
questions.explanation_text: For the fuel cell, methanol will be oxidised and oxygen will be reduced. Given reduction half-cells: $CO_{2}+6H^{+}+6e^{-} \longrightarrow CH_{3}OH+H_{2}OE_{\text{red}}^{\circ}=0.02V$ $\frac{1}{2}O_{2}+2H^{+}+2e^{-} \longrightarrow H_{2}OE_{\text{red}}^{\circ}=1.23V$ Since methanol is the fuel, it will undergo oxidation. So we reverse the first reaction: $CH_{3}OH+H_{2}O \longrightarrow CO_{2}+6H^{+}+6e^{-}$ Its oxidation potential is: $E_{\text{ox}}^{\circ}=-0.02V$ Now calculate standard cell potential: $E_{\text{cell}}^{\circ}=E_{\text{cathode}}^{\circ}+E_{\text{anode(ox)}}^{\circ}$ $E_{\text{cell}}^{\circ}=1.23+(-0.02)=1.21V$ Number of electrons transferred: $n=6$ So maximum electrical work from 1 mol of $CH_{3}OH$ is $w_{max}=nFE_{\text{cell}}^{\circ}$ $w_{max}=6 \times 96500 \times 1.21$ $w_{max}=700590J$ Fuel cell works with $80%$ efficiency, so actual work obtained is $w=0.8 \times 700590$ $w=560472J$ This work is used to compress an ideal gas isothermally against constant pressure $P=1\text{kPa}=1000\text{Pa}$ . For compression against constant external pressure, $w=P\Delta V$ So, $\Delta V=\frac{w}{P}$ $\Delta V=\frac{560472}{1000}=560.472m^{3}$ Nearest integer: $\Delta V \approx 560m^{3}$ Since it is compression, volume decreases. So strictly, $\Delta V=-560m^{3}$ If only magnitude is asked, then $560$
questions.explanation_html:
For the fuel cell, methanol will be oxidised and oxygen will be reduced.

Given reduction half-cells:

$CO_{2}+6H^{+}+6e^{-} \longrightarrow CH_{3}OH+H_{2}OE_{\text{red}}^{\circ}=0.02V$

$\frac{1}{2}O_{2}+2H^{+}+2e^{-} \longrightarrow H_{2}OE_{\text{red}}^{\circ}=1.23V$

Since methanol is the fuel, it will undergo oxidation. So we reverse the first reaction:

$CH_{3}OH+H_{2}O \longrightarrow CO_{2}+6H^{+}+6e^{-}$

Its oxidation potential is:

$E_{\text{ox}}^{\circ}=-0.02V$

Now calculate standard cell potential:

$E_{\text{cell}}^{\circ}=E_{\text{cathode}}^{\circ}+E_{\text{anode(ox)}}^{\circ}$

$E_{\text{cell}}^{\circ}=1.23+(-0.02)=1.21V$

Number of electrons transferred:

$n=6$

So maximum electrical work from 1 mol of $CH_{3}OH$ is

$w_{max}=nFE_{\text{cell}}^{\circ}$

$w_{max}=6 \times 96500 \times 1.21$

$w_{max}=700590J$

Fuel cell works with $80%$ efficiency, so actual work obtained is

$w=0.8 \times 700590$

$w=560472J$

This work is used to compress an ideal gas isothermally against constant pressure $P=1\text{kPa}=1000\text{Pa}$ .

For compression against constant external pressure,

$w=P\Delta V$

So,

$\Delta V=\frac{w}{P}$

$\Delta V=\frac{560472}{1000}=560.472m^{3}$

Nearest integer:

$\Delta V \approx 560m^{3}$

Since it is compression, volume decreases. So strictly,

$\Delta V=-560m^{3}$

If only magnitude is asked, then

$560$

questions.question_text: MX is a sparingly soluble salt that follows the given solubility equilibrium at 298 K. $MX(s) \rightleftharpoons M^{+}(aq)+X^{-}(aq);K_{sp}=10^{-10}$ If the standard reduction potential for M + (aq) + e − → M(s) is $(E_{M^{+}/M}^{\circ})=0.79V$ , then the value of the standard reduction potential for the metal/metal insoluble salt electrode $E_{X^{-}/MX(s)/M}^{\circ}$ is ______ mV. (nearest integer) [Given: $\frac{2.303RT}{F}=0.059\text{V}$ ]
questions.question_html:
MX is a sparingly soluble salt that follows the given solubility equilibrium at 298 K.

$MX(s) \rightleftharpoons M^{+}(aq)+X^{-}(aq);K_{sp}=10^{-10}$

If the standard reduction potential for M+ (aq) + e− → M(s) is
$(E_{M^{+}/M}^{\circ})=0.79V$ , then the value of the standard reduction potential for the metal/metal insoluble salt electrode $E_{X^{-}/MX(s)/M}^{\circ}$ is ______ mV. (nearest integer)

[Given: $\frac{2.303RT}{F}=0.059\text{V}$ ]
questions.explanation_text: For the metal/metal insoluble salt electrode, the reduction half-reaction is $MX(s)+e^{-} \rightarrow M(s)+X^{-}(aq)$ We can obtain this by adding the following two steps: 1) Solubility equilibrium: $MX(s) \rightleftharpoons M^{+}(aq)+X^{-}(aq),K_{sp}=10^{-10}$ 2) Reduction of $M^{+}$ : $M^{+}(aq)+e^{-} \rightarrow M(s),E^{\circ}=0.79\text{V}$ Adding (1) and (2), $M^{+}$ cancels and we get the required electrode reaction. Now use $\Delta G^{\circ}$ relation (NCERT): For equilibrium: $\Delta G^{\circ}=-RTlnK$ For a half-cell: $\Delta G^{\circ}=-nFE^{\circ}$ So, For dissolution : $\Delta G_{\text{diss}}^{\circ}=-RTln(10^{-10})=-RT(-10ln10)=10RTln10$ For reduction of $M^{+}$ : $\Delta G_{M^{+}/M}^{\circ}=-F(0.79)$ Total: $\Delta G_{\text{total}}^{\circ}=10RTln10-F(0.79)$ For the overall electrode reaction ( $n=1$ ): $E_{X^{-}/MX(s)/M}^{\circ}=-\frac{\Delta G_{\text{total}}^{\circ}}{F}=-(\frac{10RTln10}{F}-0.79)$ Given $\frac{2.303RT}{F}=0.059\text{V}$ and $ln10=2.303$ , $\frac{RTln10}{F}=\frac{2.303RT}{F}=0.059\text{V}$ $\frac{10RTln10}{F}=10 \times 0.059=0.59\text{V}$ So, $E^{\circ}=-(0.59-0.79)=0.20\text{V}=200\text{mV}$ Answer: $200\text{mV}$
questions.explanation_html:
For the metal/metal insoluble salt electrode, the reduction half-reaction is

$MX(s)+e^{-} \rightarrow M(s)+X^{-}(aq)$

We can obtain this by adding the following two steps:

1) Solubility equilibrium:

$MX(s) \rightleftharpoons M^{+}(aq)+X^{-}(aq),K_{sp}=10^{-10}$

2) Reduction of $M^{+}$ :

$M^{+}(aq)+e^{-} \rightarrow M(s),E^{\circ}=0.79\text{V}$

Adding (1) and (2), $M^{+}$ cancels and we get the required electrode reaction.

Now use $\Delta G^{\circ}$ relation (NCERT):

  • For equilibrium: $\Delta G^{\circ}=-RTlnK$

  • For a half-cell: $\Delta G^{\circ}=-nFE^{\circ}$

So,

For dissolution:

$\Delta G_{\text{diss}}^{\circ}=-RTln(10^{-10})=-RT(-10ln10)=10RTln10$

For reduction of $M^{+}$ :

$\Delta G_{M^{+}/M}^{\circ}=-F(0.79)$

Total:

$\Delta G_{\text{total}}^{\circ}=10RTln10-F(0.79)$

For the overall electrode reaction ( $n=1$ ):

$E_{X^{-}/MX(s)/M}^{\circ}=-\frac{\Delta G_{\text{total}}^{\circ}}{F}=-(\frac{10RTln10}{F}-0.79)$

Given $\frac{2.303RT}{F}=0.059\text{V}$ and $ln10=2.303$ ,

$\frac{RTln10}{F}=\frac{2.303RT}{F}=0.059\text{V}$

$\frac{10RTln10}{F}=10 \times 0.059=0.59\text{V}$

So,

$E^{\circ}=-(0.59-0.79)=0.20\text{V}=200\text{mV}$

Answer: $200\text{mV}$

questions.question_text: One half cell in a voltaic cell is constructed by dipping silver rod in $AgNO_{3}$ solution of unknown concentration, other half cell is Zn rod dipped in 1 molar solution of $ZnSO_{4}$ . A voltage of 1.60 V is measured at 298 K for this cell. What is the concentration of $Ag^{+}$ ions used in terms of $logx(x=[Ag^{+}])$ ? $E_{Zn^{2+}/Zn}^{\circ}=-0.76V,E_{Ag^{+}/Ag}^{\circ}=+0.80V,\frac{2.303RT}{F}=0.059V$
questions.question_html:
One half cell in a voltaic cell is constructed by dipping silver rod in $AgNO_{3}$ solution of unknown concentration, other half cell is Zn rod dipped in 1 molar solution of $ZnSO_{4}$ .

A voltage of 1.60 V is measured at 298 K for this cell. What is the concentration of $Ag^{+}$ ions used in terms of $logx(x=[Ag^{+}])$ ?

$E_{Zn^{2+}/Zn}^{\circ}=-0.76V,E_{Ag^{+}/Ag}^{\circ}=+0.80V,\frac{2.303RT}{F}=0.059V$
questions.explanation_text: For the cell, anode: $Zn \rightarrow Zn^{2+}+2e^{-}$ cathode: $Ag^{+}+e^{-} \rightarrow Ag$ So the overall cell reaction is $Zn+2Ag^{+} \rightarrow Zn^{2+}+2Ag$ Now, standard cell potential: $E_{\text{cell}}^{\circ}=E_{\text{cathode}}^{\circ}-E_{\text{anode}}^{\circ}$ $E_{\text{cell}}^{\circ}=0.80-(-0.76)=1.56\text{V}$ Given: $E_{\text{cell}}=1.60\text{V}$ Using Nernst equation at $298\text{K}$ : $E_{\text{cell}}=E_{\text{cell}}^{\circ}-\frac{0.059}{n}logQ$ Here, $n=2$ . Reaction quotient: $Q=\frac{[Zn^{2+}]}{[Ag^{+}]^{2}}$ Since $ZnSO_{4}$ is $1$ M, $[Zn^{2+}]=1$ Let $[Ag^{+}]=x$ Then $Q=\frac{1}{x^{2}}$ Substitute in Nernst equation: $1.60=1.56-\frac{0.059}{2}log(\frac{1}{x^{2}})$ Now, $log(\frac{1}{x^{2}})=-2logx$ So, $1.60=1.56-\frac{0.059}{2}(-2logx)$ $1.60=1.56+0.059logx$ $1.60-1.56=0.059logx$ $0.04=0.059logx$ $logx=\frac{0.04}{0.059}=\frac{4}{5.9}$ Hence, the correct answer is $\frac{4}{5.9}$ So, Option B is correct.
questions.explanation_html:
For the cell,

  • anode: $Zn \rightarrow Zn^{2+}+2e^{-}$

  • cathode: $Ag^{+}+e^{-} \rightarrow Ag$

So the overall cell reaction is

$Zn+2Ag^{+} \rightarrow Zn^{2+}+2Ag$

Now, standard cell potential:

$E_{\text{cell}}^{\circ}=E_{\text{cathode}}^{\circ}-E_{\text{anode}}^{\circ}$

$E_{\text{cell}}^{\circ}=0.80-(-0.76)=1.56\text{V}$

Given:

$E_{\text{cell}}=1.60\text{V}$

Using Nernst equation at $298\text{K}$ :

$E_{\text{cell}}=E_{\text{cell}}^{\circ}-\frac{0.059}{n}logQ$

Here, $n=2$ .

Reaction quotient:

$Q=\frac{[Zn^{2+}]}{[Ag^{+}]^{2}}$

Since $ZnSO_{4}$ is $1$ M,

$[Zn^{2+}]=1$

Let

$[Ag^{+}]=x$

Then

$Q=\frac{1}{x^{2}}$

Substitute in Nernst equation:

$1.60=1.56-\frac{0.059}{2}log(\frac{1}{x^{2}})$

Now,

$log(\frac{1}{x^{2}})=-2logx$

So,

$1.60=1.56-\frac{0.059}{2}(-2logx)$

$1.60=1.56+0.059logx$

$1.60-1.56=0.059logx$

$0.04=0.059logx$

$logx=\frac{0.04}{0.059}=\frac{4}{5.9}$

Hence, the correct answer is

$\frac{4}{5.9}$

So, Option B is correct.

questions.question_html:
Consider the following reduction processes :

$\begin{aligned} & Al^{3+}+3e^{-} \longrightarrow Al(s),E^{0}=-1.66V \\ & Fe^{3+}+e^{-} \longrightarrow Fe^{2+},E^{0}=+0.77V \\ & Co^{3+}+e^{-} \longrightarrow Co^{2+},E^{0}=+1.81V \\ & Cr^{3+}+3e^{-} \longrightarrow Cr(s),E^{0}=-0.74V \end{aligned}$

The tendency to act as reducing agent decreases in the order :
questions.explanation_text: Reducing agent is the species that gets oxidised (donates electrons). In NCERT terms: More negative $E_{\text{red}}^{\circ}$ for a couple $\Rightarrow$ the reduced form is a stronger reducing agent (it will be more easily oxidised). Equivalently, higher $E_{\text{ox}}^{\circ}$ $\Rightarrow$ stronger reducing agent . Now write oxidation potentials for the given reducing species: 1) From $Al^{3+}+3e^{-} \rightarrow Al(s),E_{\text{red}}^{\circ}=-1.66\text{V}$ $Al(s) \rightarrow Al^{3+}+3e^{-},E_{\text{ox}}^{\circ}=+1.66\text{V}$ 2) From $Cr^{3+}+3e^{-} \rightarrow Cr(s),E_{\text{red}}^{\circ}=-0.74\text{V}$ $Cr(s) \rightarrow Cr^{3+}+3e^{-},E_{\text{ox}}^{\circ}=+0.74\text{V}$ 3) From $Fe^{3+}+e^{-} \rightarrow Fe^{2+},E_{\text{red}}^{\circ}=+0.77\text{V}$ $Fe^{2+} \rightarrow Fe^{3+}+e^{-},E_{\text{ox}}^{\circ}=-0.77\text{V}$ 4) From $Co^{3+}+e^{-} \rightarrow Co^{2+},E_{\text{red}}^{\circ}=+1.81\text{V}$ $Co^{2+} \rightarrow Co^{3+}+e^{-},E_{\text{ox}}^{\circ}=-1.81\text{V}$ Now arrange reducing strength (decreasing $E_{\text{ox}}^{\circ}$ ): $+1.66>+0.74>-0.77>-1.81$ So, tendency to act as reducing agent decreases as: $Al>Cr>Fe^{2+}>Co^{2+}$ Correct option: D
questions.explanation_html:
Reducing agent is the species that gets oxidised (donates electrons). In NCERT terms:

  • More negative $E_{\text{red}}^{\circ}$ for a couple $\Rightarrow$ the reduced form is a stronger reducing agent (it will be more easily oxidised).

  • Equivalently, higher $E_{\text{ox}}^{\circ}$ $\Rightarrow$ stronger reducing agent.

Now write oxidation potentials for the given reducing species:

1) From $Al^{3+}+3e^{-} \rightarrow Al(s),E_{\text{red}}^{\circ}=-1.66\text{V}$

$Al(s) \rightarrow Al^{3+}+3e^{-},E_{\text{ox}}^{\circ}=+1.66\text{V}$

2) From $Cr^{3+}+3e^{-} \rightarrow Cr(s),E_{\text{red}}^{\circ}=-0.74\text{V}$

$Cr(s) \rightarrow Cr^{3+}+3e^{-},E_{\text{ox}}^{\circ}=+0.74\text{V}$

3) From $Fe^{3+}+e^{-} \rightarrow Fe^{2+},E_{\text{red}}^{\circ}=+0.77\text{V}$

$Fe^{2+} \rightarrow Fe^{3+}+e^{-},E_{\text{ox}}^{\circ}=-0.77\text{V}$

4) From $Co^{3+}+e^{-} \rightarrow Co^{2+},E_{\text{red}}^{\circ}=+1.81\text{V}$

$Co^{2+} \rightarrow Co^{3+}+e^{-},E_{\text{ox}}^{\circ}=-1.81\text{V}$

Now arrange reducing strength (decreasing $E_{\text{ox}}^{\circ}$ ):

$+1.66>+0.74>-0.77>-1.81$

So, tendency to act as reducing agent decreases as:

$Al>Cr>Fe^{2+}>Co^{2+}$

Correct option: D

questions.question_text: A volume of x mL of 5 M NaHCO 3 solution was mixed with 10 mL of 2 M H 2 CO 3 solution to make an electrolytic buffer. If the same buffer was used in the following electrochemical cell to record a cell potential of 235.3 mV, then the value of x = ______ mL (nearest integer). Sn(s) | Sn(OH) 6 2− (0.5 M) | HSnO 2 − (0.05 M) | OH − | Bi 2 O 3 (s) | Bi(s) Consider up to one place of decimal for intermediate calculations $⎡⎣⎢\begin{aligned} \text{Given:} & E_{Sn(OH)_{6}^{2-}|HSnO_{2}^{-}}^{o}=-0.9V \\ & E^{o}_{Bi_{2}O_{3}|Bi}=-0.44V \\ & pKa_{(H_{2}CO_{3})}=6.11 \\ & \frac{2.303RT}{F}=0.059V \\ & \text{Antilog}(1.29)=19.5 \end{aligned}⎤⎦⎥$
questions.question_html:
A volume of x mL of 5 M NaHCO3 solution was mixed with 10 mL of 2 M H2CO3 solution to make an electrolytic buffer. If the same buffer was used in the following electrochemical cell to record a cell potential of 235.3 mV, then the value of x = ______ mL (nearest integer).

Sn(s) | Sn(OH)62− (0.5 M) | HSnO2− (0.05 M) | OH− | Bi2O3(s) | Bi(s)

Consider up to one place of decimal for intermediate calculations


$⎡⎣⎢\begin{aligned} \text{Given:} & E_{Sn(OH)_{6}^{2-}|HSnO_{2}^{-}}^{o}=-0.9V \\ & E^{o}_{Bi_{2}O_{3}|Bi}=-0.44V \\ & pKa_{(H_{2}CO_{3})}=6.11 \\ & \frac{2.303RT}{F}=0.059V \\ & \text{Antilog}(1.29)=19.5 \end{aligned}⎤⎦⎥$
questions.explanation_text: For the half-cells (25 °C): (1) Sn(IV)/Sn(II) couple (given $E^{\circ}=-0.90\text{V}$ ) Balanced reduction in basic medium: $Sn(OH)_{6}^{2-}+2e^{-} \rightarrow HSnO_{2}^{-}+3OH^{-}+H_{2}O$ $E_{\text{Sn}}=E_{\text{Sn}}^{\circ}-\frac{0.059}{2}log(\frac{[HSnO_{2}^{-}][OH^{-}]^{3}}{[Sn(OH)_{6}^{2-}]})$ Given $[Sn(OH)_{6}^{2-}]=0.5$ , $[HSnO_{2}^{-}]=0.05$ : $\frac{[HSnO_{2}^{-}]}{[Sn(OH)_{6}^{2-}]}=\frac{0.05}{0.5}=0.1$ (2) Bi $_{2}$ O $_{3}$ /Bi couple (given $E^{\circ}=-0.44\text{V}$ ) Reduction: $Bi_{2}O_{3}(s)+3H_{2}O+6e^{-} \rightarrow 2Bi(s)+6OH^{-}$ $E_{\text{Bi}}=E_{\text{Bi}}^{\circ}-\frac{0.059}{6}log([OH^{-}]^{6})=E_{\text{Bi}}^{\circ}-0.059log[OH^{-}]$ Bi has higher $E^{\circ}$ , so it is the cathode . Thus $E_{\text{cell}}=E_{\text{cathode}}-E_{\text{anode}}=E_{\text{Bi}}-E_{\text{Sn}}$ Substitute and simplify: $E_{\text{cell}}=(-0.44-0.059log[OH^{-}])-(-0.90-\frac{0.059}{2}log(0.1[OH^{-}]^{3}))$ $E_{\text{cell}}=0.46-0.059log[OH^{-}]+\frac{0.059}{2}(log0.1+3log[OH^{-}])$ Since $log0.1=-1$ : $E_{\text{cell}}=0.46+\frac{0.059}{2}(-1)+(-0.059+\frac{3 \cdot 0.059}{2})log[OH^{-}]$ $E_{\text{cell}}=0.4305+0.0295log[OH^{-}]$ Given $E_{\text{cell}}=0.2353\text{V}$ : $0.2353=0.4305+0.0295log[OH^{-}] \Rightarrow log[OH^{-}]=\frac{-0.1952}{0.0295} \approx -6.6$ So $pOH \approx 6.6 \Rightarrow pH \approx 14-6.6=7.4$ . Buffer calculation (H $_{2}$ CO $_{3}$ /HCO $_{3}^{-}$ ) Henderson–Hasselbalch: $pH=pK_{a}+log\frac{[HCO_{3}^{-}]}{[H_{2}CO_{3}]}$ $7.4=6.11+log\frac{[HCO_{3}^{-}]}{[H_{2}CO_{3}]} \Rightarrow log\frac{[HCO_{3}^{-}]}{[H_{2}CO_{3}]}=1.29 \Rightarrow \frac{[HCO_{3}^{-}]}{[H_{2}CO_{3}]}=19.5$ Moles mixed: $n(H_{2}CO_{3})=2\text{M} \times 10\text{mL}=2 \times 0.010=0.020\text{mol}$ $n(HCO_{3}^{-})=5\text{M} \times x\text{mL}=5 \times \frac{x}{1000}=0.005x\text{mol}$ Ratio $=19.5$ : $\frac{0.005x}{0.020}=19.5 \Rightarrow 0.005x=0.39 \Rightarrow x=78$ Answer: $78\text{mL}$
questions.explanation_html:
For the half-cells (25 °C):

(1) Sn(IV)/Sn(II) couple (given $E^{\circ}=-0.90\text{V}$ )

Balanced reduction in basic medium:

$Sn(OH)_{6}^{2-}+2e^{-} \rightarrow HSnO_{2}^{-}+3OH^{-}+H_{2}O$

$E_{\text{Sn}}=E_{\text{Sn}}^{\circ}-\frac{0.059}{2}log(\frac{[HSnO_{2}^{-}][OH^{-}]^{3}}{[Sn(OH)_{6}^{2-}]})$

Given $[Sn(OH)_{6}^{2-}]=0.5$ , $[HSnO_{2}^{-}]=0.05$ :

$\frac{[HSnO_{2}^{-}]}{[Sn(OH)_{6}^{2-}]}=\frac{0.05}{0.5}=0.1$

(2) Bi $_{2}$ O $_{3}$ /Bi couple (given $E^{\circ}=-0.44\text{V}$ )

Reduction:

$Bi_{2}O_{3}(s)+3H_{2}O+6e^{-} \rightarrow 2Bi(s)+6OH^{-}$

$E_{\text{Bi}}=E_{\text{Bi}}^{\circ}-\frac{0.059}{6}log([OH^{-}]^{6})=E_{\text{Bi}}^{\circ}-0.059log[OH^{-}]$

Bi has higher $E^{\circ}$ , so it is the cathode. Thus

$E_{\text{cell}}=E_{\text{cathode}}-E_{\text{anode}}=E_{\text{Bi}}-E_{\text{Sn}}$

Substitute and simplify:

$E_{\text{cell}}=(-0.44-0.059log[OH^{-}])-(-0.90-\frac{0.059}{2}log(0.1[OH^{-}]^{3}))$

$E_{\text{cell}}=0.46-0.059log[OH^{-}]+\frac{0.059}{2}(log0.1+3log[OH^{-}])$

Since $log0.1=-1$ :

$E_{\text{cell}}=0.46+\frac{0.059}{2}(-1)+(-0.059+\frac{3 \cdot 0.059}{2})log[OH^{-}]$

$E_{\text{cell}}=0.4305+0.0295log[OH^{-}]$

Given $E_{\text{cell}}=0.2353\text{V}$ :

$0.2353=0.4305+0.0295log[OH^{-}] \Rightarrow log[OH^{-}]=\frac{-0.1952}{0.0295} \approx -6.6$

So $pOH \approx 6.6 \Rightarrow pH \approx 14-6.6=7.4$ .

Buffer calculation (H $_{2}$ CO $_{3}$ /HCO $_{3}^{-}$ )

Henderson–Hasselbalch:

$pH=pK_{a}+log\frac{[HCO_{3}^{-}]}{[H_{2}CO_{3}]}$

$7.4=6.11+log\frac{[HCO_{3}^{-}]}{[H_{2}CO_{3}]} \Rightarrow log\frac{[HCO_{3}^{-}]}{[H_{2}CO_{3}]}=1.29 \Rightarrow \frac{[HCO_{3}^{-}]}{[H_{2}CO_{3}]}=19.5$

Moles mixed:

  • $n(H_{2}CO_{3})=2\text{M} \times 10\text{mL}=2 \times 0.010=0.020\text{mol}$

  • $n(HCO_{3}^{-})=5\text{M} \times x\text{mL}=5 \times \frac{x}{1000}=0.005x\text{mol}$

Ratio $=19.5$ :

$\frac{0.005x}{0.020}=19.5 \Rightarrow 0.005x=0.39 \Rightarrow x=78$

Answer: $78\text{mL}$

questions.question_text: Electricity is passed through an acidic solution of $Cu^{2+}$ till all the $Cu^{2+}$ was exhausted, leading to the deposition of 300 mg of Cu metal. However, a current of 600 mA was continued to pass through the same solution for another 28 minutes by keeping the total volume of the solution fixed at 200 mL . The total volume of oxygen evolved at STP during the entire process is $____$ mL . (Nearest integer) [Given: $\begin{aligned} & Cu^{2+}(aq)+2e^{-} \rightarrow Cu(s)E_{red}^{o}=+0.34V \\ & O_{2}(g)+4H^{+}+4e^{-} \rightarrow 2H_{2}OE_{red}^{o}=+1.23V \end{aligned}$ Molar mass of $Cu=63.54gmol^{-1}$ Molar mass of $O_{2}=32gmol^{-1}$ Faraday Constant $=96500Cmol^{-1}$ Molar volume at $STP=22.4L$ ]
questions.question_html:
Electricity is passed through an acidic solution of $Cu^{2+}$ till all the $Cu^{2+}$ was exhausted, leading to the deposition of 300 mg of Cu metal. However, a current of 600 mA was continued to pass through the same solution for another 28 minutes by keeping the total volume of the solution fixed at 200 mL . The total volume of oxygen evolved at STP during the entire process is $____$ mL . (Nearest integer)

[Given:

$\begin{aligned} & Cu^{2+}(aq)+2e^{-} \rightarrow Cu(s)E_{red}^{o}=+0.34V \\ & O_{2}(g)+4H^{+}+4e^{-} \rightarrow 2H_{2}OE_{red}^{o}=+1.23V \end{aligned}$

Molar mass of $Cu=63.54gmol^{-1}$

Molar mass of $O_{2}=32gmol^{-1}$

Faraday Constant $=96500Cmol^{-1}$

Molar volume at $STP=22.4L$ ]
questions.explanation_text: Eq of $Cu=Eq$ of $O_{2}$ In electrolysis, the number of equivalents deposited and liberated are equal for the same quantity of electricity. For copper deposition: $Cu^{2+}+2e^{-} \rightarrow Cu$ , so $n$ -factor $=2$ . For oxygen evolution (reverse of given reduction): $2H_{2}O \rightarrow O_{2}+4H^{+}+4e^{-}$ , so $n$ -factor $=4$ . So, equivalents of Cu deposited $=$ equivalents of $O_{2}$ evolved during the first part. $\frac{300 \times 10^{-3} \times 2}{63.54}=n_{O_{2}} \times 4$ $2.36 \times 10^{-3}=n_{O_{2}}$ When current is further passed After all $Cu^{2+}$ is exhausted, the current now causes only water oxidation, producing $O_{2}$ at the anode. Charge passed in 28 minutes at 600 mA: $\begin{aligned} & n_{O_{2}} \times 4=\frac{600 \times 28 \times 60}{96500 \times 1000} \\ \\ & n_{O_{2}}=2.611 \times 10^{-3} \end{aligned}$ Total $O_{2}$ released Total moles of oxygen $=(2.36+2.611) \times 10^{-3}$ . Volume at STP $=n \times 22400mL$ . $\begin{aligned} & =[10^{-3} \times (2.36+2.611)] \times 22400ml \\ \\ & =111.35ml \end{aligned}$
questions.explanation_html:
Eq of $Cu=Eq$ of $O_{2}$

In electrolysis, the number of equivalents deposited and liberated are equal for the same quantity of electricity.

For copper deposition: $Cu^{2+}+2e^{-} \rightarrow Cu$ , so $n$ -factor $=2$ .

For oxygen evolution (reverse of given reduction): $2H_{2}O \rightarrow O_{2}+4H^{+}+4e^{-}$ , so $n$ -factor $=4$ .

So, equivalents of Cu deposited $=$ equivalents of $O_{2}$ evolved during the first part.

$\frac{300 \times 10^{-3} \times 2}{63.54}=n_{O_{2}} \times 4$

$2.36 \times 10^{-3}=n_{O_{2}}$

When current is further passed

After all $Cu^{2+}$ is exhausted, the current now causes only water oxidation, producing $O_{2}$ at the anode.

Charge passed in 28 minutes at 600 mA:

$\begin{aligned} & n_{O_{2}} \times 4=\frac{600 \times 28 \times 60}{96500 \times 1000} \\ \\ & n_{O_{2}}=2.611 \times 10^{-3} \end{aligned}$

Total $O_{2}$ released

Total moles of oxygen $=(2.36+2.611) \times 10^{-3}$ .

Volume at STP $=n \times 22400mL$ .

$\begin{aligned} & =[10^{-3} \times (2.36+2.611)] \times 22400ml \\ \\ & =111.35ml \end{aligned}$

questions.explanation_text: Step 1: Find $[H^{+}]$ from pH The pH is given as 5. So, $[H^{+}]=10^{-5}molL^{-1}$ Step 2: Write the relation for weak acid dissociation For a weak acid $HX$ : $[H^{+}]=[HX] \cdot \alpha$ Where $[HX]$ is the initial concentration and $\alpha$ is the degree of dissociation. Step 3: Link $\alpha$ and molar conductivity Degree of dissociation is also given by $\alpha=\frac{\Lambda_{m}}{\Lambda_{m}^{\infty}}$ Where $\Lambda_{m}$ is the molar conductivity at given concentration, and $\Lambda_{m}^{\infty}$ is the molar conductivity at infinite dilution (limiting molar conductivity). Step 4: Find molar conductivity $\Lambda_{m}$ Molar conductivity is given by: $\Lambda_{m}=\frac{k \times 1000}{[HX]}$ $k$ is the specific conductance (conductivity). Step 5: Calculate cell constant and specific conductance ( $k$ ) Given conductance (G) $=4 \times 10^{-5}S$ Cell constant $=\frac{\text{distance between plates}}{\text{area of plates}}=\frac{15cm}{1cm^{2}}=15cm^{-1}$ So, $k=G \times \text{cell constant}$ $\rightarrow k=4 \times 10^{-5} \times 15=6 \times 10^{-4}Scm^{-1}$ Step 6: Combine equations to solve for $\Lambda_{m}^{\infty}$ From above, $[H^{+}]=[HX] \cdot \alpha$ But, $\alpha=\frac{\Lambda_{m}}{\Lambda_{m}^{\infty}}$ , so: $[H^{+}]=[HX] \cdot \frac{\Lambda_{m}}{\Lambda_{m}^{\infty}}$ Recall $\Lambda_{m}=\frac{k \times 1000}{[HX]}$ Substitute in: $[H^{+}]=[HX] \cdot \frac{\frac{k \times 1000}{[HX]}}{\Lambda_{m}^{\infty}}$ $=\frac{k \times 1000}{\Lambda_{m}^{\infty}}$ So, $\Lambda_{m}^{\infty}=\frac{k \times 1000}{[H^{+}]}$ Step 7: Substitute values and solve $k=6 \times 10^{-4}Scm^{-1}$ $[H^{+}]=10^{-5}molL^{-1}$ So, $\Lambda_{m}^{\infty}=\frac{6 \times 10^{-4} \times 1000}{10^{-5}}=\frac{6 \times 10^{-1}}{10^{-5}}=6 \times 10^{4}Scm^{2}mol^{-1}$ Step 8: Convert units to $Sm^{2}mol^{-1}$ $1Scm^{2}mol^{-1}=10^{-4}Sm^{2}mol^{-1}$ So, $6 \times 10^{4} \times 10^{-4}=6Sm^{2}mol^{-1}$ Final Answer: Limiting molar conductivity $\Lambda_{m}^{\infty}=6Sm^{2}mol^{-1}$ .
questions.explanation_html:
Step 1: Find $[H^{+}]$ from pH

The pH is given as 5.

So, $[H^{+}]=10^{-5}molL^{-1}$

Step 2: Write the relation for weak acid dissociation

For a weak acid $HX$ :

$[H^{+}]=[HX] \cdot \alpha$

Where $[HX]$ is the initial concentration and $\alpha$ is the degree of dissociation.

Step 3: Link $\alpha$ and molar conductivity

Degree of dissociation is also given by

$\alpha=\frac{\Lambda_{m}}{\Lambda_{m}^{\infty}}$

Where $\Lambda_{m}$ is the molar conductivity at given concentration, and $\Lambda_{m}^{\infty}$ is the molar conductivity at infinite dilution (limiting molar conductivity).

Step 4: Find molar conductivity $\Lambda_{m}$

Molar conductivity is given by:

$\Lambda_{m}=\frac{k \times 1000}{[HX]}$

$k$ is the specific conductance (conductivity).

Step 5: Calculate cell constant and specific conductance ( $k$ )

Given conductance (G) $=4 \times 10^{-5}S$

Cell constant $=\frac{\text{distance between plates}}{\text{area of plates}}=\frac{15cm}{1cm^{2}}=15cm^{-1}$

So, $k=G \times \text{cell constant}$

$\rightarrow k=4 \times 10^{-5} \times 15=6 \times 10^{-4}Scm^{-1}$

Step 6: Combine equations to solve for $\Lambda_{m}^{\infty}$

From above, $[H^{+}]=[HX] \cdot \alpha$

But, $\alpha=\frac{\Lambda_{m}}{\Lambda_{m}^{\infty}}$ , so:

$[H^{+}]=[HX] \cdot \frac{\Lambda_{m}}{\Lambda_{m}^{\infty}}$

Recall $\Lambda_{m}=\frac{k \times 1000}{[HX]}$

Substitute in:

$[H^{+}]=[HX] \cdot \frac{\frac{k \times 1000}{[HX]}}{\Lambda_{m}^{\infty}}$

$=\frac{k \times 1000}{\Lambda_{m}^{\infty}}$

So, $\Lambda_{m}^{\infty}=\frac{k \times 1000}{[H^{+}]}$

Step 7: Substitute values and solve

$k=6 \times 10^{-4}Scm^{-1}$

$[H^{+}]=10^{-5}molL^{-1}$

So,

$\Lambda_{m}^{\infty}=\frac{6 \times 10^{-4} \times 1000}{10^{-5}}=\frac{6 \times 10^{-1}}{10^{-5}}=6 \times 10^{4}Scm^{2}mol^{-1}$

Step 8: Convert units to $Sm^{2}mol^{-1}$

$1Scm^{2}mol^{-1}=10^{-4}Sm^{2}mol^{-1}$

So, $6 \times 10^{4} \times 10^{-4}=6Sm^{2}mol^{-1}$

Final Answer:

Limiting molar conductivity $\Lambda_{m}^{\infty}=6Sm^{2}mol^{-1}$ .

questions.question_text: A solution of aluminium chloride is electrolysed for 30 minutes using a current of 2 A . The amount of the aluminium deposited at the cathode is __________ . [Given : molar mass of aluminium and chlorine are $27gmol^{-1}$ and $35.5gmol^{-1}$ respectively. Faraday constant $=96500Cmol^{-1}]$
questions.question_html:
A solution of aluminium chloride is electrolysed for 30 minutes using a current of 2 A . The amount of the aluminium deposited at the cathode is __________ .

[Given : molar mass of aluminium and chlorine are $27gmol^{-1}$ and $35.5gmol^{-1}$ respectively. Faraday constant $=96500Cmol^{-1}]$
questions.explanation_text: $\text{Al}^{3+}+3e^{-} \rightarrow \text{Al}$ The mass of aluminium deposited can be calculated using Faraday’s laws of electrolysis. The steps are as follows: Compute the total charge passed: $Q=I \cdot t=2\text{A} \cdot (30 \times 60\text{s})=3600\text{C}$ Determine the moles of aluminium deposited. Since three electrons are required to deposit one mole of aluminium, the number of moles is given by: $n(\text{Al})=\frac{Q}{3F}=\frac{3600}{3 \times 96500} \approx 0.01242\text{mol}$ Finally, calculate the mass of aluminium using its molar mass ( $M=27\text{g/mol}$ ): $m(\text{Al})=n(\text{Al}) \times M=0.01242 \times 27 \approx 0.335\text{g}$ Thus, the amount of aluminium deposited at the cathode is approximately $0.336\text{g}$
questions.explanation_html:
$\text{Al}^{3+}+3e^{-} \rightarrow \text{Al}$

The mass of aluminium deposited can be calculated using Faraday’s laws of electrolysis. The steps are as follows:

Compute the total charge passed:

$Q=I \cdot t=2\text{A} \cdot (30 \times 60\text{s})=3600\text{C}$

Determine the moles of aluminium deposited. Since three electrons are required to deposit one mole of aluminium, the number of moles is given by:

$n(\text{Al})=\frac{Q}{3F}=\frac{3600}{3 \times 96500} \approx 0.01242\text{mol}$

Finally, calculate the mass of aluminium using its molar mass ( $M=27\text{g/mol}$ ):

$m(\text{Al})=n(\text{Al}) \times M=0.01242 \times 27 \approx 0.335\text{g}$

Thus, the amount of aluminium deposited at the cathode is approximately

$0.336\text{g}$

questions.explanation_text: Electrolysis of NaCl is $NaCl+H_{2}O(aq) \rightarrow NaOH(aq)+\frac{1}{2}Cl_{2}(g)+\frac{1}{2}H_{2}(g)$ Since during electrolysis pH changes to 12 So $[OH^{\circ}]=10^{-2}$ and $[H^{+}]=10^{-12}$ So by Faraday law Gram amount of substance deposited $=$ Amount of electricity passed $\begin{aligned} & 10^{-2} \times \frac{600}{1000} \times 96500=I \times t \\ & \frac{10^{-2} \times 600}{1000} \times 96500=I \times 5 \times 60 \\ & I=\frac{10^{-2} \times 600 \times 96500}{1000 \times 5 \times 60} \\ & I=1.93\text{ampere} \end{aligned}$ So, $I=2$ ampere (nearest integer)

questions.explanation_text: Let’s analyze the situation step by step. We have 1 M aqueous solutions of: $\text{AgNO}_{3}$ with $\text{Ag}^{+}/\text{Ag}E^{0}=+0.80V$ $\text{Hg}_{2}(\text{NO}_{3})_{2}$ with $\text{Hg}_{2}^{2+}/\text{Hg}E^{0}=+0.79V$ $\text{Cu(NO}_{3})_{2}$ with $\text{Cu}^{2+}/\text{Cu}E^{0}=+0.24V$ $\text{Mg(NO}_{3})_{2}$ with $\text{Mg}^{2+}/\text{Mg}E^{0}=-2.37V$ In an electrolytic cell with inert electrodes, reduction occurs at the cathode. The ion with the highest (most positive) reduction potential will be reduced (or deposited) first. Therefore, as we increase the applied voltage (making the cathode sufficiently negative), the metals will begin to deposit in the order of their reduction potentials. The order of reduction (deposition) will be: First, silver ( $+0.80V$ ) Next, mercury ( $+0.79V$ ) Then, copper ( $+0.24V$ ) So, Statement (I) which says “With increasing voltage, the sequence of deposition of metals on the cathode will be Ag, Hg and Cu” is correct. For magnesium, the reduction potential is very negative ( $-2.37V$ ). In aqueous solution, before reaching such a negative potential, water will be reduced. The cathodic reaction for water typically is: $2\text{H}_{2}\text{O}+2e^{-} \rightarrow \text{H}_{2}+2\text{OH}^{-}$ which leads to the evolution of hydrogen gas, not oxygen. (Oxygen is produced at the anode during the oxidation of water.) Hence, Statement (II) erroneously states that “oxygen gas will be evolved at the cathode” when in fact, if magnesium were to be reduced (which it won’t be), water reduction would yield hydrogen gas. Thus, Statement (II) is incorrect. Summary: Statement (I) is correct. Statement (II) is incorrect. Therefore, the most appropriate answer is: Option C: Statement I is correct but Statement II is incorrect.
questions.explanation_html:
Let’s analyze the situation step by step.

We have 1 M aqueous solutions of:

$\text{AgNO}_{3}$ with $\text{Ag}^{+}/\text{Ag}E^{0}=+0.80V$

$\text{Mg(NO}_{3})_{2}$ with $\text{Mg}^{2+}/\text{Mg}E^{0}=-2.37V$

In an electrolytic cell with inert electrodes, reduction occurs at the cathode. The ion with the highest (most positive) reduction potential will be reduced (or deposited) first. Therefore, as we increase the applied voltage (making the cathode sufficiently negative), the metals will begin to deposit in the order of their reduction potentials.

The order of reduction (deposition) will be:

First, silver ( $+0.80V$ )

Next, mercury ( $+0.79V$ )

Then, copper ( $+0.24V$ )

So, Statement (I) which says “With increasing voltage, the sequence of deposition of metals on the cathode will be Ag, Hg and Cu” is correct.

For magnesium, the reduction potential is very negative ( $-2.37V$ ). In aqueous solution, before reaching such a negative potential, water will be reduced. The cathodic reaction for water typically is:

$2\text{H}_{2}\text{O}+2e^{-} \rightarrow \text{H}_{2}+2\text{OH}^{-}$

which leads to the evolution of hydrogen gas, not oxygen. (Oxygen is produced at the anode during the oxidation of water.)

Hence, Statement (II) erroneously states that “oxygen gas will be evolved at the cathode” when in fact, if magnesium were to be reduced (which it won’t be), water reduction would yield hydrogen gas. Thus, Statement (II) is incorrect.

Summary:

Statement (I) is correct.

Statement (II) is incorrect.

Therefore, the most appropriate answer is:

Option C: Statement I is correct but Statement II is incorrect.

questions.explanation_text: Resistance and Resistivity: $R=\rho\frac{\ell}{A}$ Where $R$ is resistance, $\rho$ is resistivity, $\ell$ is the length, and $A$ is the cross-sectional area of the cell. The term $\frac{\ell}{A}$ is known as the cell constant, $G^{∗}$ . Conductivity and Conductance: $\kappa=G \cdot G^{∗}$ $G=\frac{1}{R};\kappa=\frac{1}{\rho}$ Where $G$ is conductance and $\kappa$ is conductivity. Molar Conductivity: $\lambda_{m}=\frac{\kappa \times 1000}{C}$ Where $\lambda_{m}$ is molar conductivity and $C$ is concentration. Given Information: The resistance of the cell with the concentrated solution $R_{c}=100\Omega$ . We need to find the resistance $R_{d}$ for the dilute solution. Steps to Solution: The conductivity ratio for concentrated $(\kappa_{c})$ and dilute $(\kappa_{d})$ solutions relates to resistance: $\frac{\kappa_{c}}{\kappa_{d}}=\frac{R_{d}}{R_{c}}$ From the plot or given values (assuming values for molar conductivity): $\lambda_{m,c}$ and $\lambda_{m,d}$ are the molar conductivities for the concentrated and dilute solutions. If from the plot or data, $\lambda_{m,c}=150\text{S cm}^{2}\text{mol}^{-1}$ and $\lambda_{m,d}=100\text{S cm}^{2}\text{mol}^{-1}$ . Calculate the ratio of conductivities: $\frac{\kappa_{c}}{\kappa_{d}}=\frac{(\lambda_{m,c} \cdot C_{c})}{(\lambda_{m,d} \cdot C_{d})}$ Substituting values into the equation: $\frac{100 \cdot (0.15)^{2}}{150 \cdot (0.1)^{2}}=\frac{R_{d}}{100}$ Solving the equation gives: $R_{d}=150\Omega$ Thus, the resistance of the conductivity cell with the dilute solution is $R_{d}=150\Omega$ .

Where $G$ is conductance and $\kappa$ is conductivity.

Molar Conductivity:

Where $\lambda_{m}$ is molar conductivity and $C$ is concentration.

Given Information:

The resistance of the cell with the concentrated solution $R_{c}=100\Omega$ .

We need to find the resistance $R_{d}$ for the dilute solution.

Steps to Solution:

The conductivity ratio for concentrated $(\kappa_{c})$ and dilute $(\kappa_{d})$ solutions relates to resistance:

$\frac{\kappa_{c}}{\kappa_{d}}=\frac{R_{d}}{R_{c}}$

From the plot or given values (assuming values for molar conductivity):

$\lambda_{m,c}$ and $\lambda_{m,d}$ are the molar conductivities for the concentrated and dilute solutions.

Based on the data given below :

$\begin{aligned} E_{Cr_{2}O_{7}^{2-}/Cr^{3+}}^{\circ}=1.33V & E_{Cl_{2}/Cl^{(-)}}^{\circ}=1.36V \\ E_{MnO_{4}^{-}/Mn^{2+}}^{0}=1.51V & E_{Cr^{3+}/Cr}^{\circ}=-0.74V \end{aligned}$

the strongest reducing agent is :
questions.explanation_text: To determine the strongest reducing agent among the options, we need to consider which species most readily donates electrons (i.e., is most easily oxidized). One standard method is to compare the standard reduction potentials of the corresponding half-reactions. A lower (more negative) standard reduction potential indicates that the reduced species is less stable and more prone to oxidation. Here’s the data provided: $Cr_{2}O_{7}^{2-}+14H^{+}+6e^{-} \rightarrow 2Cr^{3+}+7H_{2}O,E^{\circ}=+1.33V$ $Cl_{2}+2e^{-} \rightarrow 2Cl^{-},E^{\circ}=+1.36V$ $MnO_{4}^{-}+8H^{+}+5e^{-} \rightarrow Mn^{2+}+4H_{2}O,E^{\circ}=+1.51V$ $Cr^{3+}+3e^{-} \rightarrow Cr,E^{\circ}=-0.74V$ Now, let’s consider the species from the Options: Option A: Cl⁻ The relevant half-reaction is: $Cl_{2}+2e^{-} \rightarrow 2Cl^{-},E^{\circ}=+1.36V.$ The reduced form here is Cl⁻. Its corresponding oxidation (the reverse reaction) would have an electrode potential of $E_{\text{oxidation}}^{\circ}=-1.36V.$ Option B: MnO₄⁻ In the given half-reaction, MnO₄⁻ acts as the oxidizing agent (it is reduced to Mn²⁺). Therefore, MnO₄⁻ is not a good reducing agent. Option C: Cr (metallic chromium) The relevant half-reaction is: $Cr^{3+}+3e^{-} \rightarrow Cr,E^{\circ}=-0.74V.$ Here, Cr is the reduced species. Reversing this reaction gives: $Cr \rightarrow Cr^{3+}+3e^{-},$ with an effective oxidation potential of $E_{\text{oxidation}}^{\circ}=+0.74V.$ Option D: Mn²⁺ In the MnO₄⁻/Mn²⁺ couple, Mn²⁺ is the reduced form. Its reverse (oxidation) potential would be: $E_{\text{oxidation}}^{\circ}=-1.51V.$ When comparing the oxidation potentials (remember, a higher oxidation potential means the species is more willing to lose electrons), we have: Cl⁻: $E_{\text{ox}}^{\circ}=-1.36V$ Cr: $E_{\text{ox}}^{\circ}=+0.74V$ Mn²⁺: $E_{\text{ox}}^{\circ}=-1.51V$ Among these, metallic Cr stands out because its corresponding reduction half-reaction has the most negative potential ( $-0.74V$ ). This negative value indicates that Cr (in its elemental form) is unstable relative to its oxidized form ( $Cr^{3+}$ ) and, therefore, is the most eager to lose electrons. In other words, Cr is the strongest reducing agent. Thus, the answer is: Option C: $Cr$

Here’s the data provided:

$Cr_{2}O_{7}^{2-}+14H^{+}+6e^{-} \rightarrow 2Cr^{3+}+7H_{2}O,E^{\circ}=+1.33V$

$Cl_{2}+2e^{-} \rightarrow 2Cl^{-},E^{\circ}=+1.36V$

Now, let’s consider the species from the Options:

Option A: Cl⁻

The relevant half-reaction is:

$Cl_{2}+2e^{-} \rightarrow 2Cl^{-},E^{\circ}=+1.36V.$

The reduced form here is Cl⁻. Its corresponding oxidation (the reverse reaction) would have an electrode potential of

$E_{\text{oxidation}}^{\circ}=-1.36V.$

Option B: MnO₄⁻

In the given half-reaction, MnO₄⁻ acts as the oxidizing agent (it is reduced to Mn²⁺). Therefore, MnO₄⁻ is not a good reducing agent.

In the MnO₄⁻/Mn²⁺ couple, Mn²⁺ is the reduced form. Its reverse (oxidation) potential would be:

When comparing the oxidation potentials (remember, a higher oxidation potential means the species is more willing to lose electrons), we have:

Cl⁻: $E_{\text{ox}}^{\circ}=-1.36V$

Cr: $E_{\text{ox}}^{\circ}=+0.74V$

This negative value indicates that Cr (in its elemental form) is unstable relative to its oxidized form ( $Cr^{3+}$ ) and, therefore, is the most eager to lose electrons. In other words, Cr is the strongest reducing agent.

Thus, the answer is:

questions.explanation_text: Let’s examine both statements one by one and see whether they hold true for typical corrosion processes (e.g., iron rusting): Statement (I) "Corrosion is an electrochemical phenomenon in which pure metal acts as an anode and impure metal as a cathode." Corrosion is electrochemical True. Corrosion, especially rusting of iron, involves oxidation at one region (the anode) and reduction at another region (the cathode) on the metal’s surface. Pure metal as anode, impurity as cathode In many practical cases (e.g., iron containing small amounts of carbon or other impurities), the relatively pure region of the iron is more active (less noble) and tends to oxidize (lose electrons) — that is, it serves as the anode. The impurity (e.g., carbon-rich region) often behaves more nobly and thus becomes the cathode region where reduction (e.g., oxygen reduction) occurs. This difference in electrode potentials between the pure region and the impurity region drives the corrosion cell. Hence, Statement (I) is generally considered true in the usual context of corrosion (like rusting of iron). Statement (II) "The rate of corrosion is more in alkaline medium than in acidic medium." For most common metals (like iron), acidic media typically enhance corrosion because abundant H⁺ ions (and possibly other acidic species) can accelerate the oxidation/dissolution of the metal. In mildly alkaline or neutral environments, metals often form protective oxide or hydroxide layers that can slow down further corrosion. While certain strong bases can attack specific metals (e.g., Al in strong NaOH), in general for iron and many other metals, corrosion is more severe in acidic environments than in alkaline ones. Thus, Statement (II) is false under normal corrosion scenarios (e.g., rusting of iron). Conclusion Statement (I) : True Statement (II) : False Therefore, the correct choice (matching these truth values) is: (C) Statement I is true but Statement II is false.
questions.explanation_html:
Let’s examine both statements one by one and see whether they hold true for typical corrosion processes (e.g., iron rusting):

Statement (I)

"Corrosion is an electrochemical phenomenon in which pure metal acts as an anode and impure metal as a cathode."

Corrosion is electrochemical

True. Corrosion, especially rusting of iron, involves oxidation at one region (the anode) and reduction at another region (the cathode) on the metal’s surface.

Pure metal as anode, impurity as cathode

In many practical cases (e.g., iron containing small amounts of carbon or other impurities), the relatively pure region of the iron is more active (less noble) and tends to oxidize (lose electrons) — that is, it serves as the anode.

The impurity (e.g., carbon-rich region) often behaves more nobly and thus becomes the cathode region where reduction (e.g., oxygen reduction) occurs.

This difference in electrode potentials between the pure region and the impurity region drives the corrosion cell.

Hence, Statement (I) is generally considered true in the usual context of corrosion (like rusting of iron).

Statement (II)

"The rate of corrosion is more in alkaline medium than in acidic medium."

For most common metals (like iron), acidic media typically enhance corrosion because abundant H⁺ ions (and possibly other acidic species) can accelerate the oxidation/dissolution of the metal.

In mildly alkaline or neutral environments, metals often form protective oxide or hydroxide layers that can slow down further corrosion.

While certain strong bases can attack specific metals (e.g., Al in strong NaOH), in general for iron and many other metals, corrosion is more severe in acidic environments than in alkaline ones.

Thus, Statement (II) is false under normal corrosion scenarios (e.g., rusting of iron).

Conclusion

Statement (I): True

Statement (II): False

Therefore, the correct choice (matching these truth values) is:

(C) Statement I is true but Statement II is false.

A $0.2%(w/v)$ solution means there are 0.2 grams of NaOH per 100 mL of solution. In 1 liter (1000 mL) there are: $\frac{0.2\text{g}}{100\text{mL}} \times 1000\text{mL}=2\text{g/L}.$ The molar mass of NaOH is approximately $40\text{g/mol}$ . First, convert the conductivity: $0.023\text{S} \cdot \text{m}^{2}/\text{mol} \times 1000\frac{\text{mS}}{\text{S}}=23\text{mS} \cdot \text{m}^{2}/\text{mol}.$ Now, convert the area units. Recall that: $1\text{m}^{2}=100\text{dm}^{2}.$ So, $23\text{mS} \cdot \text{m}^{2}/\text{mol}=23 \times 100\text{mS} \cdot \text{dm}^{2}/\text{mol}=2300\text{mS} \cdot \text{dm}^{2}/\text{mol}.$ The problem asks for the answer in the form $\text{[blank]} \times 10^{2}\text{mS} \cdot \text{dm}^{2}/\text{mol}.$ Expressing 2300 mS dm²/mol in this form: $2300\text{mS} \cdot \text{dm}^{2}/\text{mol}=23 \times 10^{2}\text{mS} \cdot \text{dm}^{2}/\text{mol}.$ Thus, the molar conductivity is $23 \times 10^{2}\text{mS} \cdot \text{dm}^{2}/\text{mol}.$

questions.question_text: Consider the following electrochemical cell at standard condition. $Au(s)|QH_{2},Q|NH_{4}X(0.01M)||Ag^{+}(1M)|Ag(s)E_{\text{cell}}=+0.4V$ The couple $QH_{2}/Q$ represents quinhydrone electrode, the half cell reaction is given below: $[\text{Given :}E_{Ag^{+}/Ag}^{0}=+0.8V\text{and}\frac{2.303RT}{F}=0.06V]$ The $pK_{b}$ value of the ammonium halide salt $(NH_{4}X)$ used here is __________ . (nearest integer)
questions.question_html:
Consider the following electrochemical cell at standard condition.

$Au(s)|QH_{2},Q|NH_{4}X(0.01M)||Ag^{+}(1M)|Ag(s)E_{\text{cell}}=+0.4V$

The couple $QH_{2}/Q$ represents quinhydrone electrode, the half cell reaction is given below:

$[\text{Given :}E_{Ag^{+}/Ag}^{0}=+0.8V\text{and}\frac{2.303RT}{F}=0.06V]$

The $pK_{b}$ value of the ammonium halide salt $(NH_{4}X)$ used here is __________ . (nearest integer)
questions.explanation_text: The cell reaction is: $QH_{2}+2Ag^{+} \rightarrow 2Ag+Q+2H^{+}$ The Nernst equation for the reaction can be expressed as: $E=E^{\circ}-\frac{0.06}{2}log[H^{+}]^{2}$ Simplifying, we obtain: $E=E^{\circ}-0.06log[H^{+}]$ Given data includes: $E_{\text{cell}}=+0.4V$ Standard potential for $Ag^{+}/Ag$ , $E_{Ag^{+}/Ag}^{0}=+0.8V$ Using the cell potential and the standard potential, we calculate: $pH=-log(H^{+})=\frac{E-E^{\circ}}{0.06}=\frac{0.4-0.1}{0.06}$ $pH=\frac{0.3}{0.06}=5$ This established pH must now relate to the buffer equation involving $NH_{4}X$ , at $pH+NH_{4}X=7-\frac{1}{2}pK_{b}-\frac{1}{2}logC$ Given the concentration $C=0.01M=10^{-2}$ , we substitute into the equation: $5=7-\frac{1}{2} \times pK_{b}-\frac{1}{2}log(10^{-2})$ Simplifying further, the equation resolves to: $pK_{b}=6$ Thus, the calculated $pK_{b}$ value of the ammonium halide salt $NH_{4}X$ is 6.
questions.explanation_html:
The cell reaction is:

$QH_{2}+2Ag^{+} \rightarrow 2Ag+Q+2H^{+}$

The Nernst equation for the reaction can be expressed as:

$E=E^{\circ}-\frac{0.06}{2}log[H^{+}]^{2}$

Simplifying, we obtain:

$E=E^{\circ}-0.06log[H^{+}]$

Given data includes:

$E_{\text{cell}}=+0.4V$

Standard potential for $Ag^{+}/Ag$ , $E_{Ag^{+}/Ag}^{0}=+0.8V$

Using the cell potential and the standard potential, we calculate:

$pH=-log(H^{+})=\frac{E-E^{\circ}}{0.06}=\frac{0.4-0.1}{0.06}$

$pH=\frac{0.3}{0.06}=5$

This established pH must now relate to the buffer equation involving $NH_{4}X$ , at

$pH+NH_{4}X=7-\frac{1}{2}pK_{b}-\frac{1}{2}logC$

Given the concentration $C=0.01M=10^{-2}$ , we substitute into the equation:

$5=7-\frac{1}{2} \times pK_{b}-\frac{1}{2}log(10^{-2})$

Simplifying further, the equation resolves to:

$pK_{b}=6$

Thus, the calculated $pK_{b}$ value of the ammonium halide salt $NH_{4}X$ is 6.

questions.explanation_text: To determine how the emf of the cell, $Tl|\underset{(0.001M)}{Tl^{+}}|\underset{(0.01M)}{Cu^{2+}}|Cu$ , can be increased, we can use the Nernst equation. The Nernst equation for this electrochemical cell is given by: $E_{\text{cell}}=E_{\text{cell}}^{\circ}-\frac{0.0591}{n}log(\frac{[Tl^{+}]}{[Cu^{2+}]})$ where: $E_{\text{cell}}$ is the emf of the cell. $E_{\text{cell}}^{\circ}$ is the standard emf of the cell. $n$ is the number of moles of electrons transferred in the cell reaction; here, $n=2$ . $[Tl^{+}]$ is the concentration of thallium ions. $[Cu^{2+}]$ is the concentration of copper ions. Given that the emf of the cell can be expressed in terms of the concentration of the ions involved, we can see that increasing the concentration of $[Cu^{2+}]$ or decreasing the concentration of $[Tl^{+}]$ will affect the logarithmic term in the Nernst equation: $E_{\text{cell}}=E_{\text{cell}}^{\circ}-\frac{0.0591}{2}log(\frac{0.001}{0.01})$ To increase the emf ( $E_{\text{cell}}$ ) of the cell, it is beneficial to have a less negative (or more positive) correction term. This can be achieved by: Increasing the concentration of $[Cu^{2+}]$ ions: This makes the term inside the logarithm smaller (since we are dividing by a larger number), which in turn makes the logarithmic term less negative. Therefore, the correct answer is: Option B: increasing concentration of $Cu^{2+}$ ions
